Tea a la Sir Andrew Clarke,

For years, whenever my Customers have asked me for a Mild Tea, I have advised the Pure. old Fashioned China which I keep, and the advice has been appreciated. It is very satisfactory to them that such an eminent authority as Sir Andrew Clarke, the London Physician, corroborates opinion. Here is an extract from an interesting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day, to the Students of the London Hospital: "Tea is a blessed beverage. Ido not know what I should do without it. But there is tea and tea, and one of the teas I have in my mind is the representation of all that is physiologically wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions here and there, and about five o'clock, when 1 get into a place, the lady of the 11011S6 will say to me : 'Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let me give you a cup of tea.' I say thank you very much.' But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, 'I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew,' and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a cup and fills thecup up with water. Now I call it positivecruelty to give tea like that to anybody and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. Tea, to be useful, should be first of an Black China Tea ; the Indian Tea which is being cultivated has become so powerful in its effects upon the nervous system that a cup of it taken early in the morning, as many do, so disorders the nervous system that those who take it actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and it produces a form of nervous disturbance, which is most painful to witness. If you want to have, either for yourselves or for your patients, tea which will not injure and which will refresk, get Black China Tea, putting in the right measure—the old fashioned teaspoonful for each person and one for the blessed pot. Then pour on briskly boiling water, and within five minutes you must pour it off again, or it will become wicked instead of good." Such is Sir Andrew Clarke's opinion and advise. A few words of warning, however, are necessary to those who have for gotten what this old fashioned tea is like. The colour of the tea after it is brewed will be found tobe much paler than that now in use, and the taste may not be acceptable at first owing to its apparent insipidness ; but if its use is persisted in, it will very soon be found to be much more suitable for the system, and if, in a week to two after its use, a trial is again made of the kind now in ordinary use, you will wonder however you could have been using it,and you will endorse Sir Andrew's statement. CUTTINGS FROM THE ANNUALS.
TRAPPED BY A FEMALE DETECTIVE.

Before one of these houses my mysterious guide stopped. Save a light in the front floor window all was darkness. To that window my guide eagerly pointed, with a look and gesture that vehemently urged instant aetion, as if a minute's delay were fatal; so I drew out and fitted a key. She was close, her lips moved, but there was no sound, not a whisper, yet into my mind, as if I had heard it, came a name —Louis Saumarez—and at that moment I opened the door and entered. What I meant to do or felt I never could put into words. My mind was concentrated on one great fact, that the murderer was in that lighted room about to escape, and that I, a woman, alone, must stop him and arrest him. One glance took in the mise-en-scene. A shady room, scantily furnished, a fire nearly out, wine and food on the table, a valise packed up,and, just drinking a glass of wine using the left hand, was a rather tall, good-looking, but sallow- faced man. Mon Dieu! I must see that other hand by some ruse. "Quo diable," said I, with a bitter but abandoned kind of manner, "Put you are a cruel lover to me, M. Saumarez." He swung round, so startled that he staggered and caught at a chair with the right hand, to which it was the nearest. I saw it full under the lamplight; a dark scar across it, the fourth finger gone! The assassin at last. "Who the devil are you ? " he demanclsed savagely. I never saw you be- fore, and you are too -- handsome to be forgotten. Leave my room. I have to catch a train, and my name is Mercier." "Pardon, Monsieur," said I coolly, my right hand on the butt of my weapon, my eyes on his ready for his attack, "you are Louis Saumarez, and you are nay prisoner for murder." I stood near the door, he at the far end of the room. At the last awful word he snatched a knife from the table with a fierce "sacre-r," and sprang towards me; but at that second I fired, and the fellow reeled back with a yell like a wounded wild beast, and fell heavily, partially stunned by the blow to his head on the floor, the blood coming from his side.—"A Twin Identity." In Belyravia Aimed.

CAPTAIN GREGORY'S LEG. It was decided that to captain should go to church one Sunday with Mary and her parents. This was to be an unofficial intimation to all whom it may con- cern that there was a purpose of marriage in the air. The captain arrayed himself gorgeously for the occa- sion, and carefully oiled the machinery of his leg. He adjusted the screws and springs, so that the apparatus would do him credit during the church service, and went forth in all the confidence begot of familiarity. The preliminary portion of the service was got over with due decorum, but about three minutes after the sermon commenced the leg gave an unexpected whirr. The captain's cough came too late for the first whirr aend too soon far the second. Then there was an un- usually loud click. This distracted the attention of the congregation from the sermon, and all eyes were fixed on the pew whence the sounds of machinery proceeded. Than a complication of clicks and whirrs was heard, and suddenly there was an upheaval of the captain's leg, which kicked a prayer book off the bock-board up to the ceiling. Then there was a paroxysm of kicking, which twisted the lee into the seat behind and knocked the bonnet and false front off the head of the -wife of the principal deacon. The leg next made an incursion into the seat on the left of that occupied by the cap- tain, and blacked a devout worshipper's eye. The captain made vigorous efforts to hold the leg still with both hands, but they were futile. The leg had gone wrong, and nothing would stop it. He cau- tiously withdrew from the seat, and proceeded to the outer air, with his leg distributing kicks and twists and flourishes and Highland flings and hornpipes all down the passage of the sanctuary. The service was resumed, but above the sound of the parson's voice,the noise of the captain's leg kicking the tombstones could still be heard. The captain went home disgusted. He tore off the leg, and ordered it to be stored away in a lumber garret. Hera, in the stilly night that leg could be heard gyrating about and distributing flings over the apartment. It got to be so sensitive of the least disturbance that if anyone closed a door- violently it would go through its entire performance.—ln "Tar diddles (Judy Annual). FIGHT WITH A MANIAC. A wan and sickly daylight was in the room when Os-tar Donelly woke suddenly to a revelation of horror which in its spectral hideousness, and its grim reality was far worse than any vision of dread that Lucilla's stories had suggested to his imagina- tion. A figure was kneeling upon the bed, erouching over him, with the strong grip of a burning hand upon his throat. A face, pallid and ghastly, was bending down close against his face, and two wild, fiery eyes were looking into his eyes. It was not till he had torn himself free from the clutch of those burninc, fingers, and had escaped to the other side of the beilstead,that he recognised his assailant as Lord Halverdene. In the struggle to free niniseit he haAl thrown his enemy from the bed to the floor. He scrambled to his feet immediately, and the two men stood looking at each other—one with a deadly weapon in his hand, the other unarmed. Oscar looked de- spairingly towards the fireplace,which was an Halver- dene s side of the bed. To reach it and get possessed of that useful weapon for emergencios,the poker, he must pass the madman, who stood at the Corner of, the bed- stead ready with his razor, grinning and muttering,. his body stooping forward like an Indian trapper lying in wait for his quarry. Ile had wounded himself in the scuffle on the bed, and the blood was pouring from a gash on his cheek. Donelly remembered that his pistol case was In a saddle-bag that had, been left in the hall. Before he could reach the hesoth to snatch the poker the madman's clutch was upon him. Oscar grappled with his foe, and then came a fight kit life, reason against unreason, the well-knit limbs and hardened sinews of athletic youth matched against the hypernatural forces of lunacy in a frame impaired by habitual intemperance. The razor, seemed every- where. It wounded both men, again and again. They were blinded with each other's blood_ Again and again Oscar threw off his foe, and made his despairing rush for door or window, but that foe was always too quick for him. Before ho could tear open. the casement the madman had him in his clutch again, and the fight had to be fought over again. Oscar fell at last, aching in every bone, bruised and battered, as if he had been broken on-the wheel; fell with Lucilla's name on his lips in the last moment of consciousness, which he believed the last moment of his life.—" The Ghost's Name." In the Mistletoe Bough.

A TRAGEDY OF THE. FJORDS. When the next evening came, Sir Patrick was very keen to try the Svara Hul again. • The sun had shone brightly and warmly during the day, whilst a strong north wind blew from the Fjord to the valley. In consequence the river had fallen considerably. Kristian looked dubious when Sir Patrick proposed that they should endeavour to repeat their luck in the same pool. "What," exclaimed Sir Patrick jestingly. "I thought you wore made of better stuff. Surely you are not afraid?" Kristian flushed a dull red beneath his sunburnt skin. He felt the taunt severely. "No," he said, slowly, "I am not afraid. I am ready to go if you wild, it. Whereupon they seated themselves in the boat, and before long they were tearing down the rapids, literally flying over the sunken boulders scat- tered along the river s bed. All at once the boat's keel struck sharply against a hidden stone, and nearly sent Kristian and Sir Patrick overboard. The former plied the oars with right good will, for the current was spinning the st.go;ttir aockitsitell round and lama, Lid 261 "She LA 'pruni,.: the situation was anything but pleasant. As had luck would have it, the right oar suddenly snapped like a twig be- neath his grasp, the broken blade floating away before he could recover it. Kristian's exertions had set the beat free, and in less time than it takes to tell she was borne towards the eddy. Ile rowed desperately with his one remaining oar, using it as a paddle, nut the stream was too strong, and he could not make head against it. On, on, they wont at sickening speed. Even Sir Patrick appreciated the danger and his fair, florid face turned a shade paler than usual. The big waves caught them—they were powerless to cross at the proper angle—and swept the boat right into the eddy. Crash! She struck the great rock in its midst, and collapsed like a nutshell beneath a pair of crackers. Her occupants were precipitated into the water. Sir Patrick felt himself being sucked down—down—down. Be struck out wildly, and as he did so his fingers came in contact with some falling body, round which they instinctively closed. Chance had flung him against Kristian, who he recollected could not swim. He clutched firmly hold of the Norwegian and then swam fcr dear life. But the eddy's horrible powers of suction prevented him from making any headway. He became faint and exhausted. A kind of vertigo was descending upon his senses. He realised that if he gave in Wit it meant death, and continued to struggle fiercely. Then he became partially unconscious, but all the time had a vague, uneasy, sensation of being whirled along like a straw, bumped, tossed, and bruised. When he came to himselt he was lying in shallow water, with his head resting on a stone, his hand still grasping Kristian by the shirt. Slowly and pain- fully he regained the shere,dragging his companion after him.—" In a Norwegian Valley." In the Christmas num- ber of London Society. • ---

"Madam," said the tramp, respectiuiiy, ;--ty— alo4e in th(; care of this house?" "Well, sir, I'm almo.it alone. I havo only the assistance of this dog and this double,-barrelled gun. Do you want anything ? " "Only to inform you that ;there may be suspicious chiracters about. Good evening, madam." "I should like to be excused, your lordship," said b, man who had been suunnoned on a jury. "What for?" "I owe a man five pounds, and I want to hunt him up and pay it." "Do you mean to tell this court you would hunt up a man to pay a bill instead of waiting for him to hunt you up?" "Yes, your lordship." "You are excused; I don't want any man on the jury Who will lie like that."

In ono Of those large and fascinating Silver. rare shops a delicious example of young girl- hood was examining nothing less romantic and dainty than fancy-buckled garters. A blonde young man with sympathetic blue eyes was waiting upon the young creature, and, though the situation might have seemed embarassing to persons not utterly innocent of mind., this sweet young girl appearerl not to be im- pressed beyond the central fact that oho desired to make a purchase. Over the glass show-case was scattered a heap of the pretty garters in every imaginable shade of silk elastic and variety of buckles. A pair of orange and black, with a curious and handsome silver clasp, had been laid to one side by the girl as being evidently the ones that most pleased her pretty eyes. While examin- ing the different examples she chatted merrily with the assistant, whose face was a pink wreath of smiles, as might be expected, con. sidering that the young lady was lovely and the conversation hinged on garters. Finally the girl decided that she wanted the orange and black pair, and she so informed him. "I want the buckles engraved with a name," Said she. "Yes," responded the young mart ; Lind what name, please I" "George," said the maiden. 11 The assistant glanced up at her face in sonle surprise, and bit the end. of his pencil contem- platively. "You —intend —these --er —these arrange- ments for a gentleman ? " he asked. "Why, of course," responded the girl, ex- panding her fine eyes and gazing upon the young man with a lustrous intensity that made him tremble.

"Ah," said the assistant. Well, as these are, of course, intended for ladies only, I was in some little doubt as to George's being able to utilize them. I will have his name put on them, howeyer. Your address, please? " There was a long pause, during which he kept his eyes cast down. Then the young lady spoke. "Perhaps," she said in a partially husky voice, " perhaps you had better put the name of Marguerite on those buckles." "Very well," responded the assistant in a gentle voice: "And will you please inform me," went on the girl, in a still huskier voice, "-where is the department for gentlemen's—er—" "Men do not wear them," broke in the clerk. "Oh," exclaimed the girl with a gasp that sounded something like a sob. And with this she made her escape, blushing like a beautiful zed rose.

CURIOUS COINCIDENCE. 7- "Waiting to see someone? " he asked of a young man who was standing on one of the porticoes of the City Hall on New Year's day. "Yes.' " So'm I. What are you after?" "I'm after a marriage license and want to see the County Clerk." "And I'm after a divorce and want to see a lawyer. Say, it's a curious coincidence, ain't U. Let's go and take a drink."

An Australian writer finds fault with the girls of Victoria for their love of slang. "Take the .cake," is not strong enough for them. They *ay, "Yank the bun." It is even said that when a gentleman asked one of these ladies if she would be his wife, she replied, "You bet your life I will."

There has been a sort of idea up to now that when a king gets the sack there is no other work that be can turn his hand to. However, that fine example of kingship, Milan of Servia, has dissipated this de- lusion. He has got a job, so they say, under the Shah of Persia as a cavalry commander. Somebody unkindly suggests that be was marked out for this appointment by his heroic achievements at Slivnitza and elsewhere ; but it is more likely that he owes It to his notorious resemblanee to a butcher.

The American dredges formerly used by the Panama Canal Company have been sold to the Nic- aragua Canal Company for the sum of £121,000 There were seven in all, but one foundered at sea in the. transfer to Greytown, and only two of thb others have been since used by the purchasing com- pany, mostly in harbour work. About 300 labourers chiefly Jamaicans, were also contracted for work on the new canal, but have generally returned to Colon, as there was no further need for their ser- vices.

Mr, Seymour LURK who at one time was.reported to be amongst the dead, has so far recovered as to be able to work for the forthcoming Lyceum pro- ductjon.,lle still looks ill, but is regaining,strength and striving to forget the Burgos railway accident. Mrs. Lucas is also designing costumes for the " Henry VIII." representation. Some idea of the magnificence with which the play will be staged may be gathered from the fact that cloth-of-gold alter a sixteenth century design is being specially manufactured for the occasion.

The Hon. Honor 6 Mercier, who has been dismissed from the Premiership o.". Quebec for corrupt rose- tices, is a Count of the Roman Empire, a Grand Cross of the Order of St. Gregory an officer of the French Legion of Honor,an honorary LLD.,a Q.C.,and a B.L. Ale has, too, we believe, received some honors from Belgium, and it is more then probable that he will now lose all his foreign honors, as well as his Canadian political influence. Four or five years ago, when he was in Opposition he was a poor man. Now he is supposed to be wealthy.

Mr. D. Lenfer Thomas, 8.A., a young barrister on the South Wales Circuit, who is a Welsh antiquarian and a sound Liberal, has made an interesting dis- covery. Lord Salisbury, at the Mansion House din- ner, stated that he was a Welshman, and Mr. Thomas has-discovered from an MS. in the British Museum that the claim arises in the following way: Twm Short C:atti, the Robin Hood of Wales, writes to Sir Robert Cecil; Lord Salisbury's ancestor, and asks him for assistance on the ground that he is his second cousin.. Commenting on this, tact, the editor of the" South Wales Star" says, "Save us from pedigrees:.

By Monday's mail we have-news of Mr. Rudyard Ripling's reception at the Austral Salon, the- " swell "club of the Melbourne ladies, where the wives of wool-kings and the daughters of golden quartz reeters meet and gossip, and listen occasion- ally to a scientific lecture by way of showing the outer world that they do note give themselves over entirely to frivolity, but are ready to improve their minds at certain not too freqnent intervals. After a programme of music and recitations, Rudyard was formally welcomed. ITe is described by one of the ladies present as, "a young, short, thick-set man, with round somewhat heavy features, very closely cropped hair, and bright piercing dark eyes,, the spectacles in front of which did not prevent the. light and sparkle being very noticeable."

in "The Woman's Harald " an incident is re-t lated about the Duchess of 'leek and her daughter,.) which is particularly interesting just now. The, story was told by Lady Wolverton. She had in- vited a large party of working-men to spend the- day at Coombe Wood and dine there.. Unfortunately it proved a very wet day, and only about twenty o'Y the expected guests arrived. It was impossible to 6 explore the grounds; so.Ledy Wolverton had largi-- fires lighted in the billiard room and picture gal• leries, and, knowing that she could depend on the. Duchess of Teck for help ,in entertaining the mem, she sent a special messenger to the White Lodgo-.. lin a very short time the popular ledy arrived wih , her daughter, and while-the former read to some of, the men in one room, the latter sang to them in another. The men were6much pleased,and declanad• that they had never spent a move. enjoyable aftaT.s- noon.

The arrest of Mr. ei W. Hastings must causa.va,. profound sensation in WOrcestensbire. Next to.tba Lord Lieutenant, he is the most important AMUR-, the county. He is chairman of the County COLIZZR, and also of Quarter Sessions ;„be is a member- of nearly every public body, and when Mr. Hastings is a member of anything he always pushes to,the front. No function:, of any kind could take place, with due dignity uinless he were present, andlhe wasregarded in fact as the Lord High Everything Else of Worcestershire. Therefore the news of the arrest must produce a social earthquake there.. He, was never popular, however; he was much too, haughty and stand-off," and there was a flavor of, Pooh-bah in his 9:4titude to everything. :Neverthe- less, he was greatly reappeted. He is the son of the founder of tha British Medical Association, anti was himself the rounder of the Social Science Con,- gress. He lives on a small estate at the foot of OA& Malvern Hills, where he has shown an • interest in dairy farming and a partiality for Jerseys.

Mr. Fred Weatherley, the well-known writer- of song-words, who is to prepare the English version of" Cavalleria,Rusticana ''' for the Carl Rosa CM- pany, is a cheery little man, with a pleasant face and small dark moustache; not a young blade madly love-smitten, as. one might suppose after reading someof his verses, but a settlad-down,.staid, married man, with a family. By profession he is a barrister, and for many years he was legal coach at Oxford. Bath his parents had strong poetic taste, but he owes most to an old gentleman who lived in his father's house who had a perfect knowledge of five or six languages,, and had been a fellow travel- ler with Scott and a friend of Thackeray. Mr. Weatheriey's songs have been as successful as any written during his time. The first he ever wrote ' were "The Past" and "The Message over the Sea," which were set to music by J. L. Roekel.. Those which caused the greatest furore, perhaps, were "Nancy Lee" and Jack's Tarn," the latter being sung just at the time the slave question was before the public.

But some unconscious sympathy might have been there all the same, or was it a presentiment rather which affected his young wife's mind. As she looked at the running water a strange. repugnance to it came upon her, aond she turned away shuddering- " I do not him to look at it, Lancelot; it is worse than the sea and the sandhills Why should it make me feel lonely and miserable all at once?" "Lb has been fatal water to more than one of ow race," Bald the baronet; "we never care to hear Yarrop Burn come down too strongly." By this time the coach had entered upon the Calierley domain, and before them stretched a long avenue of dwarfed and wind-torn beeches—a source of great family pride, as the finest specimens at anything in the shape of trees to be met with in such close proximity to the sea, for at least twenty miles along the Coast, and at the 'extremity of this avenue loomed the long, grey, stern front of Seatoe Callerley. The original edifice was strongly bail* and with genial, eanken windows • indeed, like many of the residences of Border familial, ,it ap- peared quite fitted to repel a raid, or support a siege. To this, wings of the Elizabethan • period had been since added; with, on the whole, a rather incongruous effect. Lady Callerle,y was not favour- ably impressed by her new home. It reminded her of a fortress or a prison There were no signs of welcome about, for-Sir Lancelot had forwarded strict orders thatthe time of their home coming was to be kept a- secret. &atm Nllerk.y was a place of some considerable importance•in the county, and since it had been to all hiteiats and purposes untenanted for twenty years, thoreturn of the head of the family &mom- panied fot. a young wife was an event likely to make some stir. And Sir Lancelot, who, like a good many of his race, was reserved and unsociable, did not relish the prospect of any seasonable. festivities. Stately and old-world was the entrance hall, panelled throughout with dark oak, and along with tie-usual armour and trophies formed from imple- meets of warfare and of the chase, hung half ' a dozen big sombre Callerley portraits. Each of the huge fireplaces seemed capacious enough to contain an oratory sized room, and their cosy looking bigle-nooks, with the glorious fires burning on the hearth, were the most attractive spots in the place. A lady, who was standing 'before one of these fire- plaeee, came forward with a smile, and a few words of a2tly chosen welcome. This was Dorothy Breamish, Sir Lancelot's cousin, who, lived close by at Breamish Hall, and who had made a point of being there to receive the noir comers to see that all was fitly, ordered ice, their comfort.

One Cold day in February, nigh upon the close of last century, Sir Lancelot Callerley, a gentleman belonging to a good old Northumbrian family, was bringing home his young bride. They were • approaching the end of a long and tedious journey, from London, enlivened only by ttke changes of fellow-travellers, and frequent false alarms of highwaymen. . The lumbering family vehicle which met them at the point where they left the stagecoach did not proceed with any great rapidity over the rough i country road, and n impatience of the slow pro- gress, a monstrous hat and plumes, with a very sweet faze beneath it, was frequently projected from one of the windows. This hat belonged to the bride, Lady Callerley, who was eager to catch a first glimpse of her new home. The prospect from the carriage •window appeared to her a very strange one. Her ideas of the country were limited by Twickenham and Kew, *and she had only once before been within sight of the ocean, and this was at Brighton, then the ' favourite resort of the Prince—Brighton; a very tame and sophisticated ' paradise, with its ugly pavilion and trim gzedens. In this North Country the contrast was a very marked one. Nature had it all her own way. Miles and miles of low sand- hills stretched along the coast, broken here and there by a sandstone Muff. The vegetation on these sandhills was scant and coarse, and scarcely altered the original greyish colour of the ground.. Beyond them stretched .an expellee of leaden- looking-waters, dull and greary, and monotonous in colour. What he had suffered ire this ,room in those old times--afterwards—when he was old enough to insist upon hearing familiy histories, and yet young enough to have a vivid and realist imagination! The room had a quaint old-world charm, with its stiff, stately couches and chairs its ebony and silver cabinets, its splendid, but tarnished, coves- lags, and ctutains of amber and gold brocade. Dorothy Breamish, with her fine presence and bearing, clid not seem out of place there. "Do you marvel at my hricle, Cousin Dorothy?'' t • asked Sir Lancelot, in a slew, hesitating sort of way. " She is a strange Lady Qillerley, is she not —to bring to this dismal house ?" "A strange Lady Callerley indeed !" remarkeld Dorothy Breamish, in a bane of wonder. " Whls, Cousin Lancelot, she is the merest child r "She was eighteen in May lost r "And you ? you aro forty-two," said hies. ,Breamish, thoughtfully. "I have not forgotten, or failed to take the great disparity in years into account, Dorothy;. but still, all things considered, it seemed the best thing to do, and though r am grave and sombre, she knew that quite well before she consented! I hope she may be happy, despite the difference." Oh, of course, there is small fear of that! You , are a fine handsome mane. too—but it was a risk all the same !" No wonder Dorothyßreasnish, who had expectOd to see a fine, modish, Court. beauty in her cousin's bride, was startled out of her-usual studied courteSy of speech by the first sight of this little erratum. Divested of her out-door attire and wrappings, Lady Callerley, who now joined them, and indeed overheard the last spoken-words, might have passed nite easilysfor a school girl instead of a wife; and the fashion of the dress she wore, then coming into • -vogue that fashion of affected simplicity, so opposed to the monstrously artificial one of hoop, powder, and exaggerated head-tire immediately - preceding it--favoured the impression she gave of extreme youth. She made the sweetest and most charming picture in her limp white gown, with its fiehu and tiny frill, very,full in the skirt and long behind, but short enough in front to show the pretty shoes, and with a. wide sash of yellow silk tied simply in a bow- bebised ; with ruddy curls clustering and falling negligently in that admired profusion to simulate which gave so much labottr to the hairdressers an wigmakers, but which in this case was a gift of nature. Her eyes were of that clear, exquisite blue one so seldom sees in the ayes of ' grown-up persons; there were laughing dimples lurking at the corners of her rosy lips, an. a faint colour came anch went upon the purely tinted skin. "Why. did you not inetace Breamish to come • over and dine with us also?" asked Sir Lancelot Qillerley. His cousin-shrugged her shoulders. "He is—well, Harry Dreamish's reputation L. too well known foil his wife to require to explain his absence from ler side," she returned with a laugh. "His brother Jack WaS with him when I left, and two other boon companions, Riddel of Thorneyrigg, and Forster of Nninton, so re' -was kapprenough,-methirdsa" Doubtless bl7l,- this time they will all four of ' them be unpreseatable."- The words inthemeaves were a, small reproach, . einem it wan bnnthe custom of the age for gentre- - 'nen to.drink deep s.but, in the tone of the speaker - was a contempt and disgust nearly allied .to hatred. At the . mention of her son the face of Mrs.. Breamish ebeezed suddenly. The compliment was neatly worded, but a cloud came overs Sir Lancelot's brow nevertheless. "I am-exceedingly grieved that you have given , him my•name. TITE SOUDAN REFUGEES. BOW HEN., ESCAP CP. Father Ohrwalder, Sister Caterina Chiucarine, and Sister Elizabeth Ventunini appear (telegraphs the Cabo correspondent of the "Daily News ') ex- tremely well after their prolonged sojourn in the Souda.n during whiah they suffered so terribly.. They left here eleven years ago, three years- later. were taken prisoners by the landi, and since then, I have been in Omdurman. The priest says that at tines their suffering was almost unbearable, anct when stricken down with sickness they were lin- able to obtain the bare necessaries of life. The Naha treated them most cruelly, especially the sisters, They escaped from Omdurman with the assistance. of a native, who obtained camels and planned. tha escape and fliabt to Korosko. The journey, only occupied twenfy days, The refugees repozi Oat Khartoum is in ruins `and that the RI-Jaffa is al, Omdurman with a numerous following. 144 a few are really loyal, and the priest believes; that if an opportunity occurs they would. revolt. He eeusiders that a smeell force would easily captura the whole of the Soudan. Provisions in liordd2;4, are very scarce, and prices are exorbitant. Neufeld is always chained, and Slatin Bey is a close PriSoner. The refugees know little about General Vordon beyond hearsay, having been at Opultirmall 'Oen Khar- toum fall. They have not seen any hooks or papers for eight years, and for some time past never ex- pected to enjoy liberty again. They are overjoyed at the idea of rcturning to their native country,an4 cannot realise they are free. Several Europeans arsk still at Omdurman, and though fairly healthy lead a miserable existence. ti Piga% is not at that place, and it is believed he is on his way north- ward. The Ellalifa is greatly annoyed at the taking , of Tokar.

',THE "SLEEPING BEAUTY" AT THE POBLIC HALL WYCLIFFE DAY SCHOOL Tret ANNUAL CONCERT. "The Sleeping Beauty," the legend which has charmed the fancy of childhood for ages, and has been the theme of so much speculation as to its meaningand origin by antiquarians and others, was ' the subject on Monday night of an entertain- ment which crowded the Public Rail from end to • end. The occasion was the seventh annual con- . cert in connection with the Wycliffe Day School, .• and the entertainment consisted ,el an operetta per- formed by children; it being founded on the old- • world nursery legend. and presented in such a form • as to be captivating alike to adults and juveniles., It may be said, indeed, to combine the elements of ' • an opera and a pantemine ; and to be singularly • adapted for comprehension and exposition by chil- dren. The parents of the vung performers, and • other grown up people who thronged the MI, • seemed to be SS delighted to receive from the youngsters instruction in the beautiful chapter of nursery lore, in such &highly attractive fashion as the youthful artistes themselves could have been at first having it imparted to them in theless realis- tic way at home. ,Doubtless too the children fully • appreciated the happy 'reversal of things 'whittle now placed them in the position of being the expositers of the charming fairy tale to their elders; and it must be said that they most admirably bettered the lesson. Mr. Z. Armitage, J.P., presided ever the proceedings, and pre- faced the entertainment with some observations. He • said he was happy to -say that the Wycliffe Day School was in a very satisfactory condition. It had been a plea- sure of the managers to receive a very favourable report • of the work which ha:dteen done during the year in the; school. He would not read the whole elf the report, which was a lengthy one, but it began ham very encour- aging manner, by saying that the orgameation and dis- cipline of the school :were highly eatisfentory re 4 spects, and that very good work had been done in the • elementary subjects. (Hear, hear.) They had also ob- tained a very good greent for drawing, and altogether the school was considered to be in a flourishing condition. As compared with the previous year, the average attend- ance had increased by 457, and consequently the'amount of money which had teme to the schdollfrom the Educe- tion Department was greater. The Education Act -re- • cently passed had faced in their hands power which they had taken advantage of to the fullest extent. They had been enabled to reduce the fees, and all that re- mained to make the school perfectly successful was that the parents of the scholars should aid the managerseby encouraging the regular and punctual attendance of the children at school. Without good attendanae no satisfactory 'resets could be mchieved. the other hand, with -regular attendance, and under the management of the skilled masters and their statist- ants, they had a perfect right to expect good reaults. (Hear. -hear, and applause.) 'Unhappily, they had met that night under a cloud of socrow. Had it been possible they would have adjourned the concert. Some of the audience no doubt knew that Mr. Corney, the headmaster of the school, had that day lost his little boy, and -consequently 'he was not ablate be with them, They ereust give their sympathy to the performers on that account, as /Mr. Corney had been • actively engaged for a long time in 'preparing the child- ren for the work they bad to go through that evening. His absence nughthev'e some effect upon the perform- ance, but they hoped that that .would not be the case, and that nothing would occue to mar its success. ('liear hear.) On the table in front of .him were the books which had to be given to the children for regular atten- dance at school. Their effort to encourage regillareand punctual attendance was commenced some years ago, ' by offering rewards to those who attended a certain number of times. The number of.-children entitled to receive prizes wasa94—a much greater number than twelve months ago—but in consequence of the length of performance, in which no doubt the audience were very much interested.and also in consequence of Mr. Cornev's absence,the distribution of the prizes would be postponed. He would now leave tharest of the evening in thena:nds • of the children, who he hoped would be able to furnish an entertainment that .would give esatisfaction to all. • (Applause.) The proceedings of the evening were brought toa close with the singing of the national anthem. The part a the Prince was most creditably assumed by Miss Bodth, a young lady of apparently about 17 years of age, -who comported herself with a calm dignity, and freedom from mannerism or nervousness that well be- tame the character. The Fairy Queen also acquitted herseN with much confidence, and her demeanour well beseemed the part. The style in which the perform- ance was carried out generally,save that the singing was somewhat faulty at times, was surpriclngly able; and was a remarkable xemplification of the manner in which the play-loving element in children may be taken ,advantage of to furnish an educational recreation Mit only for themselves, but also for an adult public. Mr. G. Riley was, as usual, an able accoripanist.
SILUEEFUL CRUELTY TO CHILPREN.

At Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, Thomas and Charlotte Sidebotham, of No. Stoney yard, Bank-st., were charged that they, on4the 18th inst, did unlawfully neglect and ill-treat their two children, Samuel mid Thomas John Sidebdtham, in such a manner as to cause 'injury to their health and 'unnecessary euffering.--:Mr. J. C. Sutton, clerk to the Board of Guardians, prosecuted.—Mr. B. Shearer, relieviug officer, deposed to nding thej two children inquestion, aged five and four years'; respectively, sitting on the fender beside the fire at home, covered with filth.. Inspector 'Bowen, who • was with hina,got them to stand up,ilitt they colkit. not keep on their feet,being so weak. The younger child was crying for food, and there was none in the house except some dry crusts an a basin. An elder child came in with a bag.,,to.nd the others commenced crying "buttie ;" 'tit was evident this elder ,child had been in Oho habit of dgo- ing oat begging for bread, and they knew what she had in the bag. Everything was in a filthy state downstairs, as was the naother herself, and the stench was very bad, but upstairs matters were even worse. Allem the filth was almost 'indescribable. All the furniture there was one bed, on which there • were two old bedtickings but there was neatly no bedding on these. The*Old bed tickitigs, evideCtly used by the child- ren, were covered with filth and wet. How they man- aged to sleep on them he did net know. He had known the male.defendant before and considered him a most decent n2an. The Guardians had buried one of his children for him some time since, and he had repaid every farthing of the cost. He came in while witness was at thehouse and told him ihe was employed at the gas works end only got 15s. a week, but witness learnt that he had only earned lately an average 047.123. Bd. a week.--4aspector Bowen corroterated as to the condition of things le the house.—Dr. Peacock deposed that he visited thehouse and found the two childreeconcerned sitting in a little box, and in a very dirty,condition. Their heads were filthy and the children were weak and emaciated. 'The:bed was practically an old sack filled with straw,or something else that smelt very badly,and the only eevering on the bedwras anotherold sack. The children .had been poorly withthe whoopinpcough.—Mr. Browne said he did not appear professionally in the usual way for the defendants, but merely acted tor them as a matter of ,charity. On the Court resuming on Tuesday morning, Sir Charlesßussell said he had a very distressing announce- ment to twke for himself and his learned friends repro-, seating the plaintiff. Since the Court sat on Saturday,',, certain fast: which had come to the knowledge of thel plaintiff's advisers rende,red,it impossible that they could; continue to represent plaintiff. (Sensation). Upon, these facts coming to their knowledge.hecommunieated with his learned friends representing the defendants, and stated the course which they proposed to take. They could not fiber continue to represent the ,plaintiff,and the result must, be a verdict for the defento,nts. They were acting kuot only upon the authority of Captain Osborne, butsit was not too much to say upon his imper ,ative instructions, and as plaintiff's conneit, they de- -sired to express their regrets for the reflections which, during the case, had been cast upon Mr. and Mrs. Har- freave and a third party mentioned. bir ChaKes Russell whose voice faltered as he spoke of Captain Osbcrne, said he desired tc say that throughout the whole of this matter that gentleman had acted in a thoroughly lion-: and straightforward manner! Solicitcr-General said inquiries had been made on both sides, and it was ascertained that on the 23rd of February a laxly called at Messrs. Benjamin's, in Con- duit-st., and askedithem to change £550, received from Glyn Mill4pank, into notes. Not having the notes they referred thtrlady toihe National Provincial Bank. St. James'-square, where she obtained the notes. One of these ;votes was, on an early day in March, paid by Mrs. Osborne to Messrs. Maple, in part payment of a bill. On the back of that note was her signature as Miss Elliot. Other notes had not yet been traced; but directly these facts were ascertained the result of the trial became a certainty. Mr. Justice Denman .said he had followed the case closely, and had feared some such result would be ul- timately arrived at.
A verdict was then formally agreed to for the defen- -ciants on a 1 the issues raised.

This sudden termination of the proceedings created a most profoand impression 'kit the closely-packed court. Capt. and Mrs. Osborne .did not occupy their usual place. After the verdict had beer, given the court quickly cleared.

Messrs. Spinks, in an interview with the representa- tive of the Press i.&ssociation,at the conclusion of the case, stated they were taking legal advice. as to what action they should take, as they did not see why they should suffer from the transaction. They say they have no dount whatever that Mrs. Osborne sold them the jewels. The representative of the Press Association has inter- viewed Messrs. Benjamin, whose letter to the Judge played such an important part in bringing the case to its sensational conclusion.. They expressed surprise at the suddenness of the termination, but added that they had long felt the solution of the case was to be found in the identification of the female whose gold they were asked to change for notes. Though unable themselves to iden- tify her, they deemed it their duty to give all the infor- mation they possessed.

A London Correspondent says :—Sir Charles Russell yields to a constitutional habit, which in some' degree accounts for hi brilliant success, of personally identify- ing himself with the story of his client. He believed in the innocence of Mrs. Maybrick, and worked for her with the energy of a compassionate man trying to deliver an unjustly charged woman from a shameful *ate. It was just the same with Mrs. Osborne, his 'advocacy in this case being increased by the circum- stance that she was a friend and godchild of Sir Henry Jamas, who shared hie learned friend's faith. Russell not only believed Mrs. Osberne had not stolen the pearls, but, as was shown in is powerful "cross- examination of Captain Hargrave, did not disguise:his suspicion as to tlie actual purlokier.. For this he on Tuesday morning frankly apologised, speaking with an emotitn rarely &splayed by a veteran counsel addressing the court in wig and gown. The sympathy expressed itvesurt for Captain Osborne finds universal echo outside. His faith and devotion form the may pleasant aspertin this melancholy case. It is hard to believe that further trouble is not yet in? store for him and the lady 'ho has scarcely passed be- . yond the-dtatus of a bride. It was understood in court on Tuesday that Messrs. Sak would fenthwith be reim- bursed lai the sum of £66t, of which they are at present ti losers. That would, of ceurse, stop any contemplated action,on their part, tine. the Hargreayes certainly will not move in any criminaliproceedings against their happy kinswoman. Bet the theft is undenied, and the F üblin Prosecutor is understood to te not accessible to ordinary sentiments *compassion. His duty is indeed plain. I have reason to believe tildt it will forthwith be acted upon, and The-same measure dealt out to this un- fortunate woman as-Would follow% on ordinary ease of theft perpetrated in ‘a lower social circle. It is •xulte possible that a latertelegram ma' bring information of definite action being taken by the police.

THE LATE SIR JAMES A. PICTON, CONNECPION WITH WARRINGTON. 'the life of Sir James Allanson Picton, 'one of Liverpool's most emient men, has been written by his son, Mr- J. A. Ficton, M.P. It is most healthful end stimulating, especially to young men who have akteir way to make in life. It is interesting to note that the late Sir James comes of the Pictons of Warrington. We give extracts bearing on this matterras follows : Me a reasonable inference from tombstonee and church registers that this particular family of Piektons took its name from the township of Pick- ton, near Chester, came thence to Warringtat, and toward the close of the 17th century settled at Grappenhall. near the latter town. John Fickton and. Samuel his son,of whom no 'record remains but that of birth and death, embraced considerably more than a century in their united lives, from 14:6 to 1792. The grandson Samuel, grandfather of Sir James, was a joiner and builder in Warrington. Re was a big, powerful man, more than six feet in height, and requiring shoes of a full lineal foot. His reputation is that of "a rough kind of fellow, "fond of drink,and very tyrannical." He tied at the age of fifty-seven, leaving his father still surviv- ing. The wife of this man, 'l4ary Keckwick, was a woman of much reharacter. She belenged to a Quaker family in Warrington, but after her mar- riage she becamee devoted Methodist. She was a very diligent attendant at prayer meetings, active in house to house visitations, and also eloquent in exhorting. Perhaps the reproach of the prophet might with some reason have been applied to her; "they made me keeper of the vineyards, but mine own vineyard )leaveq not kept." For she had eight children; and one of them at, least—the only one with whom the 'present writer has come into personal contact—was of opinion that their parti- cular moral welfare had been, to a certain extent, sacrificed for the salvation of souls in general ; and these children, with all their faults, were quite as well worth savingasany of the .publicans or harlots in Warrington. The following's the account given of them by Sir Jertate, and it is worth quoting : "Thomas, the eldesc,was brought up as a builder, and practised as an architect. He was for some time in London, and afterwatds superintended the erec- tion or enlargement of Haydock Lodge, Ashton, for Mr. Legh. He 'finally settled in Liverpool, where he remained until his death. Natarally he was a very able man. He could turn his hand to almost anything. He designed as an architect, engraved plates, manufactured ornamental letters for shop- , fronts. Ile: waela very accomplished musician, an admirable performer on the organ, and he made eeveral organs with his own hands. The violin or violoncello,—all -came alike to him. With all this he was a man of 'ungovernable passions, unsteady and unstable,stiCking to nothing long,very litigious and quarrrelsome He had one son, Thomas, who, when a young man, joined the expe- dition to Spain -under General De Lacy Evans,about 1825, and was never afterwards heard of. "Joseph, the second son, went to eea and entered the Royal Navy, where he rose to the rank of a warrant dicer as master carpenter. He died un- married in ISOG,,aged thirty-two. "James, the third son, also went to sea, and died young. "George lived .an the family premises, and carried on the business. remember him well when I was a child. He was a jovial, kindly man. He died in 1815, aged thirty-seven, leaving a widow without children. "My grandfather had two daughters. Sarah mar- ried a very worthy man, named Thomas Dakin. He was connected with a glass manufactory in War- rington, a very pious Methodist and 'local preacher. His wife' a big, stout, course womanewas a great curse to him. She was intemperate and violent,and eventually died by her own hand. The other sister, Mary, married a man named Marsh, a watchmaker. They settled in London, but of their .sabsequent history I know -noticing. "This brings me to my own father. Hewes brought up like the other brothers to the busineesef a joiner and brailder at Warrington. When a yoking man, as then; were too many of tee family Girths spot to make room for them all, he went to London with his brother Thomaseand remained two years work- ing at his trade. This was at a very 'bad time, toward the close of the last century, when-war was rife and trade was very stagnant. Daringa severe winter, when they could get nothing to 'do, his brother and he commenced making a model of St. Paul's Cathedral in wood, with a view of exhibiting it. They worked diligently at it for some time,but I believe it was never completed. I have some distant recollection of having, in my youthaseen some disjointed fragments of this model. "The two brothers then returned • to Lancashire At that time Haydock :Lodge, near ieshtonsin- Makerfielet, was being rebuilt for the Legh and my uncle Thomas wastappointed clerk of the works, or resident architect, and my father worked at the building. Here he became acquainted with my mother. She resided with her mother, a widow, in a cottage at liaydock, about a mile across the fields from the new building. Her grandfather, John Allanson, had come from Scotland to assist Brindley in the construction ol the Sankey Canal, about the year 1756." The marriage resulting from this acquaintance- ship was of all too short a duration; but while it 'lasted the fortunes of William fiekton prospered. For Esther Allanson, while diminutive in perecen— a physical characteristic which she was the means .of introducing for the first time into her husband's family—was morally vigorous, earnest, and com- manding. She was an excellent housewife; and while a devout Methodist, differed from her mother- in.law in being diligent in business not less than feevent in spirit. he had the art, such a happy mein clever wives, of keeping the management in her ,own hands, without appearing to domineer. There can be no doubt that the special faculties which made her son a successful and useful citizen were reainl: derived from her. Nor was her hus- band difficult to manage. Ile liked fun, and he dis- liked plodding. But he kept tolerably well to the collar so long as his home was made attraetive. And there must have been something very worthy and lovable in the nature of a man who, up to seventy years of age, was a welcome playmate to children. It var.?, not toys or sweetmeats which made him attractive to them, for he did not give them.

These are often the makeshift offerings of dried-up people who can no longer play. But he could and did play, acting the captain of the ship, or the judge in court, with a zest that took away all thought of affectation or condescension. His cheery orders to" hoist up the mainsail," or to "let go the anchor," or "port the helm," rang in the ears of his grandchildren long after; and the gravity with which from the mock bench sentence was pro- nounced on some "egregious" or "treasonable" offence oddly enriched their vocabulary.

Mr. Robert Mierpoint, wto has been adapted by the Warrington Conservatives as their candidate for, the i e borough, is a local man. He was born in War-'l, rington n, &1315 and is the eldest surviving -son of i the late Mr. Benjamin Pierpoint. Mr. Pierpoint the elder was .a.,prominent townsman, being .closety connected with important business undertakings in i the town, and he wavalso a magistrate for the borough. :and for the counties of Laneashire,and Cheshire. The present Conservative candidate-was a student:at Eaton from 1859 to 1864, and contin- ued his studies at Christ Church College, (Ward, where he took his B.A. degree in 1868, 1671. Mr. Pierpoint was called to te,.baref the Inner Temple in 1873,but he does not appear to have pursued his vocationras a lawyer very assiduously. He has, in fact,been spoken of as a" brifilless barris- ter." Whether he wanted briefs or not, is, of course, another,peestion. Lie was made a magistrate for Cheshire in 1881, and sometimes takes his seat on the 'bench at Daresbury Petty ',Sessions. Mr. Pierpoint was at one time something of an athlete, and formed one of the Christ Church College." eight." He was also captain of the shoot- ing " eleven " at Eton. As he mentioned at the nseetingof the Conservative Council last-week, he has travelled in fotsign countries pretty ostensively. He Las4isitedEgypt three times, and haajourneyed through- the Holy Land, and paid several visits to Italy and France. His residence is lit. Austin s, Warrington, and he is a member of the Wyndham Club, Bt. James's-square, and also of the Liverpool Consemative`Clab.

With the 31st December closes the second year of the existence of the above association, with fairly-satisfactory results, taking into account the large area covered by the operations oft the organi- sation. In theitrst place, the central council have been instrumental in preventing the pollution of the rimer Duse.i and steps are being taken to secure the establishment of a Rivers Conservancy Board, covering the whole of the district traversed by the rivers Aire and Calder and their tributaries. There his also,been.prepared with the sacrifice of consi- derable time and ttouble, a memorial toithe London and 11•Torth-Western, and Lancashire and Yorkshire Railways, praying for increased facilities for tn.-, vellingder anglers, under conditions which,,will practi- cally secure the proper use of any concessions granted. The mennorialsesigned by nearly 6,000 persons, are now in the hands of companies, and it is hoped the Directors may accede -to the wishes of the memorialists. The local Council of Alike above centre have also-been actively engaged during the present year, and have succeeded in obtaining. through the kindness of Mr. Keldrum, a cheap list ef return fares, to angling resorts.in West and North-Cneshire,rDerbyshire, and Lincolnshire, and tra- velling,cards for the use of members will be issued, pro- bably, late in January of the coming year. Negotiations have also been.opered with Mr. E. LeaderiWillliams, engineer to the.alancliester Ship Canal Compay, with a view to acquiring that portion of the Runcorn and Latchford canal.b6etween Walton Arches and Moore as a reservoir‘tor.fish, and the experiment of turning fry and yearlings intonit,-is to be made; and if succeasful, steps will be ,taken-during next summer, to placeanglers on a proper footing .with the Canal Company. "This, we believe, will providenmple sport for all lovers of the gentle art in the.district, in the near future. erhe pol- ' lution of the Dare between the 6th and leth of the pre- sent month, has-resulted in the total destruction of all , fish life in that stream, between Middlewich and !Korth- i wieh .1 the Weaver below Northwich will also have suffered conEiderably. It is satisfactory to notiee that the Mina SanitarrAteilarity, have promptly -taken the matter inhand, with the result that a Local Govern- ment Boardiniviry.was held at Middlewich on Decem- ber nth., and in- this way the pollution Alias been traced to its source. .The angling clubs of Northwieh, Middlewich, Warrington. and Manchester, have remleted considerable aid to the Cuthority, in producing %wit- nesses to giveavidence on the abundance of ish in- the stream. The result of the inquiry has not yet been made known, but we believe that steps are being taken to prevent a recurrence. The association urges-upon every angler in-the district, the necessity of uniticf, their forces in the coming year, In order to carry .eurt the many reforms needed to improve their position, andf appeal more especially for pecuniary aid, both dor the parent association and the district centre.

div.p: lANDUM DRIVIN'.

'Twuz on that Greyt Elekshun Day,— (In th" Bull's" warm Snug aw heerd the tale)— Wen him ez wuz Sir Ruchert Cross Powt liurnul George McCorkodale. Three gradely rum 'uns geet on spree, An' rowlt aw o'er th' owd place at random, Wen aw at oncet they catcht two mokes, An' yoket um up fer drivin' tandum. King Dick, ez seem'd quite natteral, Wuz soon appinted Boss o'th' job; Wile Cocktail, nothin' loth fer larks,' Wu x helpin', summut like a 'lob.' "Lobelia George" lookt after th' lush, An' kept a teet hond upo' th' tap; An' wen he thowt they'd hed enough, Mootht after harness an' a trap. By eyow ! sum sarious chaps abeawt, Thowt they'd gone smack bang off their wits; Wile some o'th' wimmin livin' near, Laaght thersels in convulsion Ats I Well, off thay seet, fro' th' "Bull," an' went I To th' " Crow "; an' just a thay pood up, Sir Ruchert an' his chaplain passed, Ad' Dick invited urn to sup! Bat " Ruchert," bein' pusht fer,, time, Sed, wi' a twinkle in his eye, " Excuse me, friends, mi mate an' me Er bed a quart, an' arend dry." Then, off agen, to th' powlin' booth, To gie ther favorite a lift.; But, wo ! howd on! not one darn'd hoof Them bloomin' quadroopeds would shiftl Thay kickt, they backt; thay jumpt, thay An' th' leader stood reet on his yed ; Wile th' shafter, not to be eawtdun, LAM deawn, ez if he war i' bed! Dick swore, an' wen he'd gen ther ribs, Wl' an' owd swippa, mony a jow, Roar'd eawt to Cocktail," Hook it sharp, An' tee sum carrots to a pow." ‘Twuz done, an' wen thay howdet th' bunch in front o' oather Neddy's nose, Thay bawkt," anutber weyver dead," buukt' for cecrrcts,bet rKt blows! Well, tiler's a morril i' my tale, Thet fits fer ey'ry greyt occasion; " Virhen'eer yo've jackasses to drive, Don't pummil urn, but try Persuasion." So„ here's a Merry Krismus, lads; To aw, full pockets, au' full skins; In' don't fergeti' ev‘ry race, Wi' men or mokes, .Persuaslon wins! TIIM 0' PEGS. NTowton God bless o'.

div.p: DROWNED AT STRETFORD.
ALL
NRADE MRI‘I,

On Wednesday morning, Mr. F. Price, county coroner, held an inquest at Patricroft, on the body of William Henry Stott, 18 years of age, a bcathoise driver on the canal, who lived with his parents at 4, South View Teel Greetcßoad, Barton. On IVlondayevening the deceased was in charge of a horse drawing a boat laden with coals on the Bridgewater Canal. The night was very foggv, and the deceased fell into the water and was drowned. A verdict of accidental death was returned. A LAMPLIGHTER FROZEN TO DEATH. On Wednesday morning Thos. Winder, aged 70 yew, of Broomhill, Wombwell, near Barnsley, was found dead at Broomhill. The deceased was a ,lamprnan, employed by the Wombwell Local Board, and on Tuesday nigkl, went his usual-round to extinguish tile lamps. He did not return, and his son gong in search found his father dead on the roadside. The deoeased had evidently been seized with a fit, and falling down was frozen to death. POUR BOYS DROWNED NEAR BURY. On Wednesday afternoon as a number of boys were skating on a mill ledge at Stubbing, near Bury, the ice gave way and four were drowned. Their names are James Howarth (1.1), James Greenhaugh (12), George Howarth (l 6 and Wm. Watson (10). TWO BROTHEB.S DROWNED AT WLLKDEN. A sad drowning fatality occurred at a village named Walkden, near Bolton, on Tuesday afternoon, two brothers, named William and Charles Bennison, aged respectively eleven and nine years, being drowned. Whilst sliding on a large reservoir near their home the younger boy .lipped through the ice, and theelder one, in attempting to pull him out, was also dragged in. Their cries were heard by a local schoolmaster, Mr. Wal- ler, who went to their rescue and got them out. The ,younger boy was dead, argi2l the other died in ,a school ,close by soon after. BOY DROWNED IN CHESHIRE.

A respectable youth, aged 14 years, named Butrows, whose parents reside at Wrechury Heath, Cheshire, met with his death on Tuesday under distressing circum- stances. He was sliding on a pond near his home along with a few lads, when all at once the ice gava way, and he was precipitated into the water. Before any assist- ance,,could be rendered he was drowned.

div.head: LATE MR. M. BOWDEN.
div.p: THE LATE MR. M. BOWDEN.

The funeral of the late Mr. M. Bowden, grocer, Sankey-st.,took place at the Warrington Cemetery, on Monday afternoon. The death of Ur. Bowden took place on the previous Friday." afternoon, and although he had been unwell for some time the death was rather unexpected. It took place at his residence Overton, Frodsham. Mr. Bowden was a, prominent Wesleyan, and had held many offices in I connection with that body. Ile was also at one time a member of the Board of Guardians, an over- seer for the borough,and had also been a candidate for municipal honours. On Monday the body was conveyed from Overton by coach, and the funeral procession was met in Wilderapool-causeway. Among those present at the grave side were—Mr. James Bowdon, Stretford, brother; Mr. F. W. Bowdon, Liscard ; Mr. A. Bow- den, Mr. W. Bowden, and Mr. R. Bowden; Mr. J. W. Swift, Warrington, brother-in-law; Messrs. It. Cook, A. H. Dunn, J. Toft, I. Biddle. J. W. Hayward W. Parkinson, and J. Shaw Green, trustees of the Wesleyan Chapel, Bewsey-road, Warrington; Mr. E. Place, Mr. W. Winstanley, and Mr. I. Hayward, officials of the chapel ; Mr. E. Mitchell, Messrs. J. B. Isaac, J. liartles, S. Moss, J. Gandy, J. Johnson, J. Bayley, and Mr. T. Evans. The service was impressively read by the Rev. Alfred Freeman, one of the circuit ministers. The inscription on the coffin was" Matthew Bowdon,born December 4,1832; died December 18, 1891." Several floral wreaths had been forwarded by sorrowing relatives and friends.
WARRINGTON WESLEYAN CIRCUIT.. QUARTERLY MEETING.

This meeting was held at Bold-st. Chapel, on Monday. A. substantial tea was provided and pre- sided over by Mrs. Richardson and Mrs. W. Silcock, the circuit stewards' wives. A large number of church officers were present from town and country, After tea the chair was taken by the Superinten- dent of the Circuit, the Reif. John Gunnell, who was supported by his colleagues, the Revs. A. Free- man and T. Ross. Mention was made by several gentlemen of the great loss Methodism had suffered 1 by the death of Mr. Matthew Bawden, who had filled almost every office in the Warrington Circuit open to laymen.; and it was resolved that a letter of sympathy be sent to Mrs. Bowden and family. The financial statement of the stewards was emin- ently satisfactory, showing a balance in hand of £26. The chatT.man reported the number of church members to be 690, an increase on the quarter of 20, with 50 on trial for church membership. The following officers were thanked and re-appointed : Messrs. E. Richardson and W. Silcock, Circuit Stewards; Mr. Lawton, Treasurer of Circuit Travelling Fund.; Mr. R. Cook. Circuit Chapel Secretary ; Messrs. J. Shaw Green and W. Silcock auditors of foreigii mission accounts. A very hearty vote of thanks was also given to the local preachers for their valuable pulpit services throughout the 'circuit. An interesting conv&sation arose on the report of a special committee appointed by the September quarterly meeting to consider the read- justment or increase of the ministerial appoint- ments in the principal country chapels. It was decided to secure if possible, a young unordained minister to reside at Penketh who should give special pastoral attention to Penketh and other country placos. The meeting, while gratified by the large number of young people who are members of the Bandvof Hope in various parts of the circuit, regretted that so little temperance work was being done among the adult members of the congrega- tions; and a small committee was appointed, with the Rev. T. Ross as secretary, to devise measures for consolidating and extending the temperance cause in all the congregations of the circuit. The annual united trustee meeting was fixed for March 21st.
TERRIBLE DYNAMITE EXPLOSION.
SEVERAL LIVES LOST.
Lloyd's Antwerp agent telegraphs :—The pilot boat iin Kattendyk Dock has been destroyed by a dynamite explosion. Several vessels were damaged, and several persons killed and wounded.
WRECK OF A STEAMSHIP.
LOSS OF NINE LIVES.

SAN FRANCISCO, WEDNESDAL —The steamship West Coast, Captain Gerne, has been wrecked off Point Arenas, and is a total loss. The captain, a fireman, and three sailors were rescued, but a Nat containing ten men capsized, and the two engineers, the two mates, the ;cook, a cabin boy, and three sailors were drowned.

div.head: TRE BRIGHTON MURDER.
div.p: TRE BRIGHTON MURDER.

The inquest on the body of the little girl, Edith Jeal, aged five, who was found murdered and fearfully out- raged in a shed on December 10th. was resumed on Sat- urday evening at Brighton--Dr. Humphreys, surgeon, deposed to having been called to the shed, and there finding the body of the child. The child appeared to have been strangled. The jury returned a verdict of wilful murder against George Henry Wood.
SENTENCE OF DEATH AT GREENOCK.

At the High Court, Glasgow, on Monday, Frederick Thomas Storey was charged with the murder of a circus performer named Elizabeth Stewart, otherwise Lizzie Pastor, at Greencck, on the 14th ult. The prisoner had been in the employment of Mr. Cooke, circus proprietor, for 14 years, but was dismicsed several days before the tragedy for indulging in drink. For the defence it was held that the accused was of unsound mind at the time. The jury found him guilty of murder, but recommended him to mercy. Lord Adam passed sentence of death.
DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT STROOD.
NARROW ESCAPES.

A destructive fire broke out on Wednesday night on the premises occupied by Mr. Frank East, draper. Strood. An assistant, in lighting the gas, set tire to the Christmas decorations in a window, and so rapid was the spread of the flames that it was with the utmost difficulty the as- sistants and the customers saved their lives by running out at the back door. Two of the shops were gutted, and the stock in other shops adjoining was greatly damaged.
THE APPROACHING ROYAL MARRIAGE.

It is understood that the ceremonial at St. George's Chapel, Windsor, on the occasion of the marriage of the Duke of Clarence and Avondale with Princess Victoria May of Teck will follow as far as possible the arrange- ments of the wedding of the Prinee and Princess of Wales. The Duke of Clarence, who has been the guest since Saturday of the Dake and Duchess of T:ck, at White Lodge, Richmond Park, returned to Marlborough House at one o'clock on Monday, and will remain over Christmas with the Prince and Princess of Wales. The Duke of Clarence and Princess Mary and the Duke and Duchess of Teck were on Tyesday in Richmond Park, where thousands of skaters were enjoying them- selves on the frozen ponds. The Duke of Clarence later in the day drove to Marlborough House.
SHOCKING SUICIDE AT GQUORNE.

Mrs. Hurst, the w.ife of Mr. HUtst, proprietor of the Queen Anne Hotel, Golborne, committed suicide on Wednesday morning under particularly painful circumstances. About eight o'clock, as her hnsband was about to leave the house with the intention of purchasing some milk, the deceased came down- stairs. On being questioned by her husband as to the reason why she came down at that unusual hour' she replied that she required some " salts. ' He, being satisfied with the answer, departed on his errand. On his return he found that Mrs. Hurst had retired to her bedroom. Shortly after there was a loud crash in her apartment, and on going to ascertain the cause, he found the door of the room in which his wife was, was locked, and on receiv - ing no reply to his queries, Mr. Hurst, becoming ap- prehensive, had the door burst open, and to his horror found the body of his wife, with her throat cut, lying in a pool of blood. There was a butcher's knife, smeared with blood, at her side. The deceased has been suffering from insomnia, and this, it is be- lieved was the cause of the rash act.

A FEW years ago the Princess of: " Cruel Wales made. a, dead-set at.what was SporVr. then the. fashionable pastime of. pigeon-shooting; and:now the Queen herself has caused a. letter to be written to Colonel Coulson " exprossing her symrathy with his efforts to put an encitothe cruel sport of rabbit coursing." We welcome this letter as.. something • which will set people thinking, and ,givean impulse in the right direction ; but at the, same time we cannot but won- der that her Majesty- does not recognise that her disapproval should go, further and:; include stag- hunting with the Woyal Buckhounds. The periodi- cal accounts of the hunt of the tame stag which is kept for the purpose, cannot but excite feelings of repulsion and even: of disgust in the minds of the. majority of her najesty's subjects. Grantectthat itis brutalising to set dogs upon rabbits 'to chase and kill them, itis surely no worse than hunting la tame stag with buckhounds,, hour after hour,. ;and finally casting the exhausted brute horse ?alive in order that it may; be hunted, again t.: -.:There is a refinement of meanness awl cruelty in this " royal " performance which is. utterly beyond the, reach of the vulgar parsons who indulge in the vulgar sport 2,,f rabbit-coursing. It is to be hoped the discussion of the subject which is going on in the press, will result in her Majesty hearing something of the.zelation botw.een a mote in one eye and a beam in another, and that in the end she will set her face against" cruel sport " of every kind. And that what is usually meant by sport is cruel, who will venture to. deny? When Burns saw a woundea bare limp by him he invoked a curse upon the " inhuman " sportsman, his "bar- barous art and" murder-aiming eye." He spoke es a right-minded and right-feeling man; and if it were not that custom so often blinds people, the sentiment would be a common one. Our children are taught the fable of the boys and the frogs, without reflecting, it would seem, that the moral —" what is sport to one may be death to another" —applies to hunting, angling, bird-snooting and rabbit coursing as well as to stone-throwing in a frog-pond. When men hunt, and fish, and shoot with the object pure and simple of obtaiaing food supplies, or destroying pests, they may be said to be legitimately 'and warrantably occupied. It is when these things are done for " sport" that the wrong commences—wrong which may difter in
degree, but is entirely of the kind which is con- demned in the fable of the frogs.

A good deal is heard from time to tinwr of the tortures of vivisection, but we do not hesitate to say that more cruelty is inflicted in a single day in the hunting or shooting season than is caused in a whole year in this country by vivisection, restricted as it isby the law. This will be a new point of view, perhaps, to some sportsmen who go out with a fowling-piece and "murder-aiming eye;" and, after " potting " a number of birds, or rabbits, sign a petition for the, total suppression of vivisection. But let them think the matter out, and ask themselves seriously if maiming and kil- ling for " sport " is as defensible as maiming and killing with the object, of advancing scientific knowledgeand ameliorating the lot of mankind. Anglers, it may be conceded, do not stand in the ordinary catgory of sportsmen,; and it maybe that they have some sort of warrant for speaking of theirs as" theg,entle art." It• is gentle as compared with hunting; gentle in its- soothing relation to nature in her loveliest aspects by strearwand• wood- land ; but by no means gentle-in relation to the fish. Granted that the finny denizens- of the waters have a low' and (relatively) insensitive- or— ganisation, it is absurd to suppose that it doesnit hurt them to be dragged by hook + and line out of their element. Byron certainly did • not take this. rosy view of the matter, and he turned the tables, sharply.on Isaac Walton, when he said :

The quaint, old, cruel coxcomb in his gullet,. Should have a hook and a small trout to pull, it. much, it will be observed, dewnds upm the! point of view; and, going back to the Queen's, letter, what we have to.urge is that, if rabbit-- coursing is to be condemned as cruel,, other sport 123t113t also be condemned—not excepting stag- hunting with the Royal Ruckhounds. Cowper is whit old-fashioned as a poet; but he is:ever to be honoured for saying—

I would not enter on my list of friends,„ Though graced with polished manners- and fine sense? Yet wanting sensibility, the an Who needlessly sets foot upon a worm. An inedvertent step may crush, the snail, That crawls at evening in the public pa, But he that hath humanity (forewarned), . Will step aside and let the reptile live.

There are many sportsmen, we are psed to thinkrwho•step aside in the spirit and letter a_ theselines ; and when next they do so let them take to, considering why they should spare the. snailondi-for sport, kill a pheasant, a rabbit, or a hare.

Ls T Sunday was what is known as Waco Sunday, and in a large num-- , • ber of places of wor&iip throughout :the-country special sermons were preachedibn the horrors of.war and the blessings of peace,- It is-, 'fitting that this should be done on the advent of : Christmas-tide ;and it is also fitting;_that it should
P6acur Sunday.

be done-on many Sundays throughout the year. There ismo denying that the clergy have neglected their duty in this respect; and it appears, as the Rev. C.. E:AKzn3 of Liverpool, put it, on Sunday, that the-world will have to look to the federation of "the democracies of Europe for adoption the

_ principles of the Prince of Peace rather than to Christian churches." It seems to some people - like imagining a vain thing to suppose that the time will ever come when.: the: na-- tions - shall loam war no more; but. if 1 these people!, had the question put to them-- "-Why should; meni fight ?" they would probably.. find a iifficulty in givin an answer.% It ist.re-.- garded as evidence,of brutality and bad training when.indiyiduals.attern t to settle diffokonees,byb- brealling each others ea s. They are very peo-- perly told that there are courts of law and jgdges, and juries to determine disputes of every possible kind. .But why. not. go a step further and say. there shall be International Courts to settle interna— tional disputes ?.• From our point a view, it; is, justas,muclbevidence of brutality and bad training:. for nations to, fight as for individuala; :and when the democracies of the world are enlightenedlandi bettertorganisedi they will take care-- that.; they - are notiused as food for powder merely to gratify- __
_ the pride, p_assions, and caprices of raonarchsiandi statesmen.,
liard Russell once said—" On 100 king at all thee wars. which ,have been carried on during -the. last
century, 3.rrel ex:amining into the causas,of them,. IL
db. not see .one of tha wars in which,,if there ,had

been preeer temper between the parties, the ques- tions in disput I ought not to have been settiedwith out ecourse•to arms." How sad, how appalling it 'is, to think: that a lack of " proper temper" should 'have been the means of causing the•loss of tens of thousands of lives and the destruction of property which is-only to be estimated by millions II when there was ,a cause of dispute between two nations the iswae•was referred, in due formeto an rntorna- tional Court of Arbitration, the temper. which sa often: steps in and causes mischief weuld have timetocool, and would not, at any rate),be likely to have much influence over the njudicially-minded men,who would be selected as arbitrators.. But it is sometimes asked—How are• time decisions of such a court to be enforeed,? And if they are.enforced, does not that in itself mean war With regard to the first point, the answer is that: those who agree to refer a dispute to arbitration, should also agree to abide by the result, whether- ' framer against them. What is most required is the, disposition on the part of strong nations to tenst, to powerful reasons rather than powerful =pa.- 'merits. Mr. GLADSTONE set. a noble example in dealing with the Alabama claims. His conduct was denounced at the time by the Tories, buteeven they have come to reco- nise that it resulted not only in justice being done, but in averting what would haeo been a terrible war between regland and the I,lnited States.. The feeling in favour of arbitration is un- doubtedly growing, and it would be well if candi- dates at the next election were questioned as to their willingness to vote in favour of cheeses being inserted in all new treaties with the, object of re- ferring to arbitration all disputes. which may arise out of these treaties. Assuming that there will be such a thing in the future as a Permanent International Court, backed by all the great, rowers, it is surely obvious that there would be little difficulty about enforcing decrees. The Power that resisted would be as much a law- breaker as the individual who resisted the decree of a Court at home; and would be dealt with accordingly. A single Power might bluster ' and show fight ; but it would be as helpless against "the world in arms "as a single individual would be in the hands of half-a-dozen policemen. Sol- diers would thus become international police; and, as such, their operations wouid be attended with more real honour and less vain-glory than at pre- sent. The existing system of ever-increasing arma- ments is happily in danger of breaking down from its own enormous weight. We are raising in this country close on 90 millions annually, and by far the greater portion goes in paying for past wars, or preparing for future wars. Why should we
