div.head: TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: TOUCH AND GO."

The bulk of the Tory members of the Corpora- tion of Liverpool have dishonoured themselves by declining to confer upon Mr. Gladstone the freedom of the borough. "It is worse than a crime—it, is a blunder," seeing that the greatest .Englishman of the age had his birthplace in Liverpool. 'ILYSV will it look a hundred years hence, when.,.the incident has to be dealt with by the historian?

One for Bismarck: The other day the Social Democrats called a meeting with the avowed object of asking the ex-Chancellor to resign his seat in the Reichstag. When the meeting was held, it was found that Prince Bismark's supporters were in a majority; and they turned the tables on his opponents by carrying a vote of confidence. This is something like what has happened when Liberal Unionists have held open meetings--they have found themselves in a ridiculous minority.

There is talk of sending the Duke of Clarence to Ireland as Viceroy; but we cannot think it is anything but talk: If it were proposed to be done, it would be merely as a Government move in view of the approaching tieneral Election; and 'the Prince of Wales is too wide-awake to permit of his eldest son being used in this way. Any idea that it would have an appreciable .effect in conciliating the Irish people is absurd; they are not just now to be "pleased with a rattle:--tickled with a straw."

Mr. T. W. Legh, the member for the Newtonl Division, is not to have a "walk over" as he seems to have anticipated. A Liberal candidate is now forthcoming in the person of Mr. W. Nellie, barrister, who addressed the" 300," and was well received on Saturday. From all we hear, he• wilt' make a good fight; and, if the Liberal electors -" buckle to " and support him as they ought to do, he will have an excellent chance of winning the seat. The Tories were beaten in the County Coun- cil election, and they can be beaten at the General Election.

Dr. Bardsley from being Bishop of Sodor and Man is promoted to be Bishop of Carlisle. In an I interview with a journalist, on Tuesday, he ex- plained,amongst other things, that the Isle of Man income was about £1,500 a year, whilst the income of the Carlisle Bishopric was £4,500; "so that," he added, "it is really a good thing." Just so, and yet again, just so. When a workman gets his wages raised 300 per cent. at a stretch, there can be no gainsaying the fact "it is really a good thing." It is enough to "make the mouth water" of the hard-worked and underpaid curate; and he is to be found everywhere.

The pressure of foreign competition is causing something like a revolution in the plate-glass trade of St. Helens. It is not that the St. Helens manu- facturers are ready to "go under " ; on the con- trary they are preparing to meet competition by adopting the latest methods and machinery: This will involve large outlay; and it will be seen how important is the change contemplated when it is stated that it is expected to quicken the processes of grinding, smoothing and polishing to such an extent as to complete them in one day instead of three days as at present. Some details of the pro- posed changes will be found in another column.

Two gipsy fortune-tellers have been sent to pri- son for a month each, for following their ",profes- sion ;" they were trapped by policemen's wives. One fortune-teller "charged each of the women is. and told them that she could rule the planets, and turn all their bad luck into good, but for that they Would have to pay her a little more." Of course; who wouldn't pay a trifle more to have bad luck turned into good? And then think of the planets being ruled for the ridiculously low sum of one shilling! Odd though that the fortune-tellers didn't see that the gaol door was opening for them. Perhaps the ruling planets were for once unruly P

Mr. Stead must be crdited with having sug- gested at least one new idea in the "Review of, B,eviews ; " and that is that the violence of the inevitable collision between the House of Com- mons and the House of Lords, on the subject of Home Rule, should be broken by some "form of Referendum to the Christian people of Great Britain and Ireland." But wouldn't the remedy be worse than the disease? It might end in a " form of Referendum" to the police. No, better "have it out" with the Lords; and, as to them, it is to be hoped they will resist it to the death—to the death that is of the Lords as hereditary and irresponsible legislators.

It is one of the difficulties of the "comedy man" that he cannot be taken seriously when he wants to be. Toole can be pathetic as well as funny; and it sometimes happens that his pathe- tic touches raise a laugh from the undiscerning when they should produce a tear. Mark Twain suffers in the same way; he is a believer in the thought-waves which are known as telepathy, or mental telegraphy ? Some years ago he wrote a grave article on the subject; but he did not dare to publish it, lest it should be taken as "kinder sarcastic." But he has issued it now when the subject is exciting attention, telling people in effect that it is not to be laughed at.

Lord Abergavenny, a Tory peer of more than average influence, has been raising his voice in presence of a member of the Government (Baron de Worms) against the Irish Local Government Bill. This, following on the revolt of the Tory Conference, is suggestive of the deep dislike to doing anything for Ireland. The effects of the breeze which has set in will be worth noting. The Government know there are rocks ahead; and it may suit them to strike on this particular rock. They could make a show of bringing in the bill, taking care to let the Liberals defeat it, and then appeal to the country. It is an old game, and it may be played again.

Roman Catholics are not as a rule given to ex- pounding the doctrine that there is salvation out- aide the Church of Rome ; but Cardinal Manning does not hesitate to speak out on the subject. In a recent review, he says :—" We believe that the • Holy Spirit breathes throughout the world, and gathers into union with God, and to eternal life, all those who faithfully co-operate with His light and grace. None are responsible for dying incul- pably out of the visible Body of the Church. They are only culpable who knowingly and wilfully re- ject its divine voice when sufficiently known to them." This leaves a loophole of escape for the average Protestant, though it is not a very large one.

The tale of corruption in American politics seems to grow blacker every year. Some details are to hand of a contest in Clinton county during which votes were openly bought, the price gradu- ally rising under the competition of Democrats and Republicans from £1 to £4 per vote, at which latter price, it is stated, the Democrats "secured at least 90 per cent. of the floaters." " Floaters " is a good word; it is so expressive, and comes so trippingly on the tongue. There are floaters in this country, and they used to fetch a high price. Their numbers have been greatly lessened by the Corrupt Practises Act. Pity the floaters and those who float them cannot be tied together and sunk.

Touching the hat nuisance, a nice point of law has been raised in the United States. The mana- ger at the Grand Opera House, Minneapolis, is sued by a theatre-goer because, his view being obstructed by two large hats worn by ladies in front of him, the usher on complaint being made refused either to find another seat or refund the entrance money. The case at present stands ad- journed, but; if the plaintiff succeeds, what an opening for litigation is afforded! It might end in managerial restriction as to the size or the wear- ing of hats in the Opera House. In the mean- time, ho I, would it be if the man who finds the

ST. AMBROSE CHURCH, WIDNES. Recently Miss Ganthorpe of Birkdale,Southport,placed a memorial tablet in the church it memory of her family who were formerly residents in the parish. This is the first tablet placed in the church. GAS FITTINGS.—J. S. Garland, Gas Fitter, Bridge-st., Warringtou.—Advt.

STREET ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN. Whilst walking on the footpath opposite Mr. Steels's shop, High-st., on Monday afternoon, an elderly woman named Mrs. Evans, slipped on a piece of ice, and fell breaking her leg at the thigh. The woman was removed into Mr. Banks shop, over the way, and P.C. Crowder rendered first to the injured woman who was afterwards taken on a police ambulance to her house in Cartwright- at. and attended by Dr. McDougall. PETROL:WM Ou..—J. S. earland, Ironmonger, Bridge-St.,

Warrington.—Adrot. PRESENTATION AT THE GREENWAY-ROAD BOYS' SCHOOL. At the " breaking up "for the Christmas holidays at the above school, on Wednesday, Mr. W. Stubbing, assistant master, who is leaving this Christmas, was presented with two beautifully bound volumes of Words- worth's and Moore's poems, bythe teachers and scholars. Mr. Stubbing in thanking those who had subscribed to the presentation, said that he should remember with pleasure, his connection with the school. Mr. Moulton suitably replied on behalf of the assistants and scholars. EMIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the " Examiner " Office, by Cunard, Onion, American. Aus- tralian, Oriental, and other lines.—John Walker, agent. " Examiner" Office. Bewsey-st.. Warringten.—.Advt. MURDHROUS ASSAULT ON A WIFE AT WIDNES. Before Mr. Timmis and Mr. J. Birchall, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Michael Gorsr,han, of Rose- street, was charged with assaulting his wife Ellen. The prosecutrix said she had been married to the defendant -rtyr-ea-yetre. On Wednesday morning while they were in bed he kicked her and she got up and dressed. The prisoner had previously threatened so take her life and she was afraid to live with him any longer, and she asked for a separation order. The evidence was not deemed sufficient to grant an order, but the prisoner would be bound over to keep the peace for six months. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. tt W. Durrol,Sankey-street. Warrington.—Advt. PRIZE DISTRIBUTION AT DUTTON.

The annual distribution of prizes given by the Dutton School Beard took place on Wednesday, in the school- room. Mrs. Hervey Talbot, of Dutton Lodge, kindly attended to present the books, and for each child she had a cheerful word of praise and greeting. The master thanked Mrs. Talbot for the great interest she had al- ways taken both in the Sunday and Day Schools, and the children seconded this by giving three hearty cheers. In reply, Mrs. Talbot said that she should always be happy to help the school in every way she possibly could. The scholars were theft dismissed for the Christmas vacation. KITCeEN RlNGER.S.—Gariand Builders Ironmonger, ‘War rington.— Advt. HOLY TRINITY DAY SCHOOLS, RUNCORN.

These schools broke up for the Christmas holidays on Wednesday, and in the evening a magic lantern enter- tainment was given to those scholars, who, during the past month had made ninety per cent. of the total at- tendances possible. Mr. Edgar Lea was the exhibitor, and splendid views of South Africa and the Diamond Fields and Gold Diggings were thrown on the screen. The popular story " Jack and the Beanstalk" was then Klustrated,and the entertainment concluded with a num- ber•of comic slides. Mr.'r. H. Annett, the head master, graphically described the views, which highly delighted the children. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.-3, and W. DuTrox. Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. WHY THE THIEF CAME TO RUNCORN. At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Mr. Brun- drit and Mr. Handley, a convicted thief named Jos. Warren was charged with having on the previous day stolen a pound of butter the property of George Pa rtington,grocer, High-st.; and also ajar of jam belonging to Edward John- son and Co., Church-st. Mr. Lancaster, partner to Mr. P?rtington saw the prisoner steal the butter,but captured him and recovered the butter. Later a police constable saw the prisoner steal the jam and took him into custody. He was sentenced to 21 days' hard labour on each charge. It transpired that the priSoner had only teen released , from gal on Friday, and asked why he had come to Run- corn said the Prisoners' Aid Society had paid his fare to 1 Acton 'Bridge. LANDLORD AND LODGER AT RUNCORN. At Runemn Police Court, on Wednesday, a Ship Canal labourer, named William Owens, was brought before Mr. Brundrit and Mr. James Handley to answer a charge of assaulting Isaaac Mannion, of 3, Anchor-st.—Owens had lodged with Mannion, who on Monday morning told him he would have to find a fresh place.—Mannion alleged that Owen thereupon used bad language, struck him violently in the face, and threw him to the ground. The defence was that Owens when he received this summary notice, asked to be allowed to go in and get some "chuck," but Mannion refused and attempted to force him off the promises.—The magistrates considered that Owens had been dealt with summarily by Mannien and ordered him to pay the costs 10s. 6d. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W.PUTTON, Sankey-st. Warrington.—Adrt.

------- CHDRCH SALE OF WORE AT WIDNES. The annual sale of work in aid of the funds of St. Paula Church Sunday and Day Schools was opened on Wednesday afternoon by Mrs. H. S. Timmis. The sale was held in the boys school of the National Schools and the Rev. G. H. Garrett, 8.D., vicar, in introducing Mrs. Timmis to perform the ceremony, said it was now 30 years since the Waterloo-road schools were built, although they had been considerably enlarged since that time. During the last 25 years the schools had made rapid strides, which was largely due to their excellent headmaster, Mr. Crawford, who had been connected with the school that length of time. With regard to the Sunday schools which were such an important branch of juvenile work, he asked for their special help in order to provide prizes to encourage the children to attend regularly.—Mrs. Timmis then declared the sale open and on the proposition of the Rev. R. Meiklejohn, seconded by the Rev. W. S. Jones, a vote of thanks was heartily accorded to her. Mr. H. S. Timmis responded on behalf of his wife.—The sale then commenced. The stalls were in charge of the following ladies :—St. Marys day school stall; Mrs. Crawford, the Misses Crawford and Misses Parker, Wilson and Cave. St. Mary's Sunday school: Mesdames Garrett, Brookes, Farrant, Misses Davies, Walker and Benbow. St. Paul's Sunday school : Miss Deacon and Mrs. T. Hughes. Refreshment stall: Misses L. Davies, Fogg and Baker. There were also two Christmas trees in charge of Miss Fairly, Sc. Jones, Tinsley and Dwerryhouse. lIMBRELLIS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adv.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 26, 1891,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 26, 1891,

SALE OF THE HAWARDEN CASTLE AT RUNCORN. Mr. S. Yarwood,auctioneer, on Wednesday afternoon, at South Bank Hotel, offered for sale the screw steamer, Hawarden Castle which foundered on the Formby coast about three week's ago. The vessel was built in 1881 by Messrs. Ferguson and Baird, C3nnahs Quay, and had new engines put in last year at great cost. The vessel which was owned by Mr. Rowlands, of Runcorn, was knocked down to Messrs. John Gibney and Co., Liver- pool, for £470. CHEMICAL WORKERS' HOLIDAY. The men in the chemical works of the United Alkali Company in Widnes, St. Helens, and else- where, received notice that so far as the manufac- turing proCesses are concerned, they would cease work on Wednesday night, and the works will be stopped until Monday, the 4th of January. UMBRELLAS ItECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-it., Warrington.—Aevt. RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT NINTWICH. What might have resulted in a terrible railway accident occurred at Nantwich on Wednesday. At 12 o'clock the Bristol express ran through Nantwich station and mounted the hill beyond. The driving rod snapped, and with the revolution of the wheel the rod struck the rails. A number of chairs were seriously damaged, and the permanent way was considerably damaged Fortunately the mishap was detected and the train pulled up. A delay of about an hour occurred before an engine from Crewe ar- rived to take on the express.

Mr. Bowver manipulating the machine. At the conclu- sion each boy was presented with an orange.

A CHILDREN'S BAZAAR. The. above schools " broke up "for the Christmas holi days on Wednesday, and in order to make the event more enjoyable for the scholars, a children's bazaar was held in the afternoon in the Girl's School. The opening ceroivony took plac..; at half-past two, and among those present were Dr. McDougall and Mr. Moss, clerk to th 3 Board. The bazaar was declared open by Dr. McDougall, Who congratulated the scholars on the progress they were making, and spoke in terms of praise of the work of the teachers. The stalls. were decorated in an attractive style, and were laden with both ornamental and useful The sales proceeded very rapidly, and the•re- iresinnent stall, .as last year, was particularly well patronised. Much praise is due t 6) Miss Kilburn, the head mistress, and her assistants Miss Simkin, Acton, Perkins and Ellison, for the very effective manner in which all the arrangements were carried out. The receipts realised upwards of £4, which will be devoted to the scholars" prize fund.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN'
AT RUNCORN, &c.
"Br AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."

- - About the last tradesmen one would expect to see charged with selling adulterated food would be the Co-operative Societies which exist in nearly every, Lancashire, and in many 'Cheshire towns. The representatives of Runcor;Co-operative Society had the unpleasant experience of appearing before the magistrates on Monday, to answer two separate charges of selling yeast adulterated with 15 per cent. of starch, and coffee adulterated with 10 per cent. of chicory. The defence was that the yeast was purchased as pure,and was sold as received,and that the coffee was put up for the inspector from papers plainly bearing the intimation that it was a mixture of coffee and chicory, although the packet he carried away bore no such inscription. As the customers at the Co-operative Stores participate in the profits at the end of each half year, there can be nothing gained by palming impure articles upon them : and one can, therefore, the more readily be- lieve that there was no such intention in this case. At toe same time, when an article i 5 asked for, it should be supplied, and it is a good thing for the public that the Legislature has passed laws to pro- tect them as far as possible from consuming adul- terated food. The Bench of magistrates took a le- nient view of the matter,.and fined the defendants in the lenient penalty of ss. and costs in each case, and did not call upon the defendants to pay the fees of the analyst, which is usual,aud which amounted to two guineas.

An olcl lady fell on the pavement at the corner of Church-st., this week and fractured her leg, and she was carried to a shop over the way. As usual a crowd quickly gathered and it was thought that the woman had fallen through the shocking condi- tion of the footpath at that part of High-st., and the words that were spoken were far from compli- mentary to our Board of Commissioners. Fortun- ately the lady had slipped throughA piece of ice, or perhaps there might have been an action for dam- ages. It is a crying shame that the footpath in the principal thoroughfare should nave been left in a half finished state for so many weeks, and there must be mismanagement somewhere. Who is to blame? The too long holiday granted to the chemi- cal labourers this Christmas tide was the prin- cipal topic at a public meeting in connection with the Chemical and Copper Workers Union at Widnes on Sunday, Mr. Keir Hardie,a miners' repre- sentative said the works are to be closed for a fort- night simply to keep the prices up, as the scarcer an article became the higher price was obtained by the masters. It was the same with labour, if the people were willing to work under present circum- stances their condition !would never be improved, and he advocated eight hours a day. Mr. King, the autocrat of the Union, said if every man in Widnes became a member they would not have these long holidays at Christmas, or they would know the reason why.

-- There is no doubt this prolonged stoppage of the works has created much dissatisfaction amongst the men,who regard it as a great hardship. It is one more black mark placed against the syndicate,which is held responsible for much that has taken place since its formation. The men would have borne the stoppage with more equanimity had it occurred in midsummer when the pinch of poverty would not be so keenly felt, but in this severe, though season- able weather, an insufficiency of fuel in the human boiler soon makes itself felt throughout the whole system. However I hope the managers will be en- abled to act on the suggestion I made last week,and make advances to those who are in need, which could be repaid when they rhsumed work. Other- wise it is feared that the relieving officers will have a very busy time of it and the rates will suffer.

Apropos of the meeting mentioned Mr. King made the announcement that for every member in benefit the union was worth £4 per head, an d stated that this fact would startle • \-en his own Committee. I always understood that the Committee of an organ- isation managed the affairs and were the repository of all the secrets. Is not, this so in the Chemical Workers Union? A resolution in favour of an eight hours working day was unanimously carried by the chemical workers ou Sunday,

I was glad to see that Mr. Edwards, of Frudsh au' had repented of his declaration not to fulfil his duties of Guardian after his defeat on the Frodsham Water question. He was amongst those present at the meeting last week and took as keen an interest in all that was going forward. Perhaps the com- plaint of his "Senior" overseer (Mr. Davies) had something to do with the breaking of his vow, and Frodsham having its full representation again.

The dispute between the two overseers mentioned is a very pretty one. There is no banking account kept of the township monies,and while 24r. Edwards demands one to be kept and refuses to sign the rate book until that is done, Mr. Davies on the other hand refuses and says he cannot be compelled to keep one. Personally I think the request for a banking account a most reasonable one and ought to be conceded at once. Before a deadlock ensues through the dispute, a ratepayers' meeting ought to be called to settle the question.

understand that at their next meeting Runcorn Board of Commissioners will adopt a memorial simi- lar in tems to the one adopted by the Widnes Local Board, respecting the proposed Vehicular Bridge across the Mersey. They also intend to enlist the sympathy and support of the vario,is townsmen on the Cheshire side within a radius of several miles of Runcorn, and from what I hear they will be suc- cessful in their appeal for aid in petitioning the County Council. Widnes Local Board could not do I better than follow suit on the Lancashire side. By the way of putting the cost of the Bridge at £250,000 which is £lOO,OOO more than the estimate it would cost the two counties considerably less than a penny in the .£, and the advantages gained would be enormous.

At the last meeting of the Widnes School Board it was determined to abolish fees in the infant depart- ments of the Board Schools. The chairman (Mr. T. Sutton Timmis) wished at the same time to deal with the fees charged in the upper standards, but it was ruled that this could only be done after due notice had been given, and it was therefore intended to hold a special meeting to discuss the matter. I understand that this idea has been abandoned and that the present system will be allowed to exist until the end of the March quarter when action will be taken.

-- A few weeks ago Mr. James White, a prominent Conservative in iVidnes,wrote to a local contempor- ary showing by figures the excellent condition of the Tory party in Widnes Division, and the great enthusiasm that prevailed amongst rank and file. Although Mr. Deacon with his unsullied character and tremendous local influence was a very strong opponent, they had no fear of his unseating the present member, Mr. Moss. This enthusiasm was conspicuous by its absence at a public meeting held in the assembly room of the Conservative Club the other evening, when Captain Lewis was announced to deliver a lecture on " The Unionist Government, and its claim to support." Considerably past the advertised time there were about nineteen persons present all told, including the Chairman, Mr. Richd. White, and a party of 13 whom he had brought from lialebank. Captain Lewis however, gave a well thought out and argumentative address. But where, oh where ! were those enthusiastic Tories?

MR. DEACON ON IRELAND AND THE LABOUR MOVEMENT. Mr. H. Wade Deacon, Liberal candidate for Wid, nes Division, speaking at a meeting in connection with the Widnes Division Liberal Association, at Woolton on Friday night said: The Unionist family was not so happy as it appeared to be; the leaders wanted to do one thing and their followers another. One matter which Lord Salisbury dwelt a great deal on was the priestly influence in Ireland, and he stated if Home Rule was granted there would be a general revolu- tion. He (Mr. Deacon) did not defend undue ecclesias- iastical interference, but he thought • that that they had ecclesiastical interference and intolerance in our own country. He did not wish to hurt the religious suscep- tibilities of any man, but still hefelt that he must speak out on this subject. Lord Salisbnry had said that the priests had such an influence that they could turn a national organisation from one side to another as a man turned a boat by the rudder. He (Mr. Deacon) wished to compare this view with that of Lord Spencer, who undoubtedly had more experience of Irish affairs than Lord Salisbury. Lord Spencer said that such statements as these were greatly ex- aggerated, and that it was wrong to think that. Home Rule would mean home Rule. The people in the country places often had no advice to seek but that of the Priest, and under the circumstances the priests were almost forced to study politics. In Ireland there had been twelve Protestant members of Parliament returned; and in England only four Roman Catholics. According to these figures, there was less religious intolerance in Ireland than in England. Lord Salisbury prophesied terrible things, but that was the usual habit of the lory party. There was nothing in these prophecies that should prevent the friends of Ireland assisting their great leader to have the command once more, and to instil new life and energy into the Irish nation. The speaker then dealt with the agricultbral labourers, and stated that some people said they did not affect those in the town. This was wrong, as the whole country was bound to be affected by the agricultural labourers. At present there Was a tendency for them to leave the land and go to towns, but it was the intention of the Liberal party to endeav- our to keep them on land by providing something to interest them in the villages. Another question which was agitating the minds of the labouring classes was the number of hours they ought to work, Many were in favour of only working eight hours, and receiving the same pay as at present. If the hours were reduced, and the wages remained the same, it Would, in many cases, necessitate the employer closing his works. It was impossible to pass a universal law which would be applicable to all trades alike. The working-men were responsible for the solution of this problem, but the strong must regard the weak; if they did not then they must suffer. They acknowledged this when the poor law was passed ; this law had lifted many from the low degraded lives which they were living. Then it was a national duty to regard the weak; and who were the weak ? The agricultural labourers. If the country was to prosper they must regard this class, as the land was a source of all their wealth. (Applause.) A resolution of confidence in Mr. Gladstone was passed.
RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY.

STABAT MATER. To judge by the audience who assembled in Run- corn Public Hall on Monday evening, there is no falling off in the interest taken in the performances of Runcorn Musical Society. The body of the hall was well filled, nearly every seat being occupied, but the listeners in the gallery were far more select than numerous, and it is a matter for surprise that those for whom the lowest fee is charged should remain indifferent to the exceptionally fine musical treats which the society has in the past provided. However, there was no doubt a paying " house " and the audience was thoroughly appreciative, with- out being unduly enthusiastic. The first part of the programme consisted of Rossini's " Stabat Mater," and the principals engaged were Miss Monteith, soprano; Miss Sarah Berry, contralto; Mr. Edwin Houghton, tenor, and Mr. A. S. Kinnell, bass. The orchestral band and chorus numbered 150 performers. In former con- certs the band has been a great attraction and a source of unqualified enjoyment, and speaking of their per- formances on this occasion the same praise must be be- stowed, but taken on the whole the band was far too heavy for the strength of the choir, whose voices in more than one chorus were drowned by the combined sound of brass reed and string. Of course it must be at once admitted that the choir suffer under a serious disadvantage in the fact that they are placed in a recess, which detracts much from the force and volume of their singing. Having taken these preliminary objections, it cannot be denied that the choir, on the whole, sur- mounted their difficulties admirably and the concluding chorus "In sempiterna siecula " was a most admir- able and enjoyable piece of work. The principals rendered the various solos with much ability and it is unnecessary to particularise each item. Both Miss Monteith and Miss Berry received unanimous encores, the former for the air (and chmus) " Infiammatus," and the latter for the cavatina " Fac ut portem." Miss Berry is practically a new star on the musical horizon, and,gifted with a contralto voice of far more than ordin- ary range, combined with dramatic power and expLes- sion, she at once gained the sympathies of her audience, and in her several apprearances she was enthusiastically welcomed. Miss Monteith is the possessor of a soprano voice of rich quality, and she sang with much power and feeling. Mr. Houghton made his first appearance before a Runcorn audience, but it is to be hoped it will not be his last. His vocalisation was of a high order of excellence, and his voice is pure, strong, and mellow. Mr. Kinnell has a voice of pleasing quality, and he sang the several items to his name with taste, but wanting in power and energy. The second part of the pro- gramme was of a miscellaneous character, and opened with the overture " Zampa," by the band. At a later period the hula also gave the grand selection" Carmen" (Bizet). Both of these selections were brilliantly per- formed, and were long and loudly applauded. The part song "Now tramp" (Bishop) in which Miss Monteith took the solo, was admirably rendered, and both chorus and principal deserved the hearty plaudits which followed, An enthusiastic encore rewarded Mr. Hough- ton for "An evening song," and he responded with "When other lips." "The enchantre:s " gave Miss Berry every opportunity for a display of her powers, and she was recalled three times, when she sang" The minstrel boy." Miss Monteith narrowly escaped an encore for her feeline rendition of "A night divine." The appropriate song "Christmas comes but once a year," was given by Mr. Kinnell, and the concert ended with God save the Queen," in which the chorus and band took part. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, the hon. conductor, wielded the baton with his usual ability, and Mr. J. NV:Collins= again proved a capable leader of the band.

RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY AND ADULTERATED FOOD. At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday before Mr. James tiindley and Dr. Steele, George Powell, manager of the Halton-road branch of the Co-opera- tive Society, was summoned on two informations with having sold on the 12th November adulterated yeast and coffee.—Mr. W. J. Hallard, inspector of weights and measures for this part of the country, and his, assistant proved the purchases. The analyst (Dr. Carter Bell)certified that the coffee was adulterated with I ten per cent. of chicory and the yeast with 15 per cent. of starch. The analy,st stated that no champ had taken place in the sample of yeast that would interfere with the analysis. Mr. Fletcher, of Northwich, who defended on behalf of the Co-operative Society, said the object of the Society was to provide as far as possible pure food for members who associated together,and they would be the last persons in the world either to mislead or to perpe- trate a fraud on their customers. There ought to besome discretion exercised in the way in which these prosecu- tions were instituted by those who had to take them,and if a little discretion had been used in this case, it might have prevented the society being brought before the court and subjected to the popular notion that they had done anything wrong or unworthy of honest traders. The yeast was French yeast, which was well-known in the market, and was imported by the firm of Wilkins and Company, who supplied it to the Wholesale Co-operative Society, Manchester, who then supplied the Runcorn Co-operative Society. It had been used by the Society for 15 years without complaint. In their cata- logue Messrs. Wilkins represented it as pure and the bags were also marked "Guaranteed pure" and although this was perhaps not sufficient warranty to satisfy the statute, still dealing with the case on its merits, this was sufficient to prove that the society believed they were selling a pure article. Fifteen per cent. of starch might be necessary for the manufacture of the yeast. As to the coffee, it was for the convenience of the poor classes taken out of two packets, each showing that it was a mixture of coffee and chicory, and this explanation was given to the in- spector on the same day. (The wrappers of the coffee were handed to the Bench). There was clearly no in- tention to defraud, and he said this was an unfair pro- secution to take advantage of a blunder. This was manufacturing offences,and it was not the way the duty of the inspector should be diszharged. Officials should rather help tradesmen to obtain honest articles, and warn them when they were selling articles which were not quite pure—W. Morris, assistant man- ager, stated that this Society had a written warranty of the purity of the yeast but he had not been able to find it.—Mr. Thomas Pearson, one of the managers of the wholesale society, having given evidence, Mr. Handley said the magistrates thought Mr. Fletcher's clients had failed to comply with the Act in both cases. The sectien stated there must be a written warranty, and the article demanded had not been supplied.—Mr. Fletcher : The smallest coin of the realm would satisfy the demands of justice. We have not been guilty of any crialinality whatever.—Mr. Handley: If you had allowed me to finish it would have saved you these remarks. There will be a fine of ss. in each case and the Co urt costs 10s. 6d.

div.head: LIVERPOOL SUNDAY SOCIETY.
div.p: LIVERPOOL SUNDAY SOCIETY.

The weekly meeting of the Liverpool Sunday Society was held on Monday,in the Rotunda Lecture flail. Mr. F. H.Gossage.J.P., presided, and there was the usual large attendance.—The Chairman, in the course of his introductory remarks, said that was the first time he had taken the chair on an occasion of that sort, I4e was, however, an extremely strong supporter of that society, and there was no doubt about the good it was doing. He wished to con- gratulate them on the triumph they had gained in the opening of the Walker Art Galimy. The first rung of the ladder had been won, and if they con- tinued working with the same energy and persever- ance, he had no doubt of the result. He wished them all a merry Christmas, and he hoped they and the society would have a prosperous New Year.—An excellent programme of songs and recitations was rendered by Mr. and Mrs. Wallis A. Wallis, two very talented entertainers. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. SHOCKING FATALITY AT A WIDNES WORKS. On Thursday afternoon Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at Widnes Acci- dent Hospital on the body of Patrick Mcliew. 43 years of age, who had resided in Warrington-road. The dkeased was employed at the British Alkali Works and on Monday evening at half-past five he commenced removing saltcake together with three other men. At half-past ten was seen to throw down his shovel and walk towards the end of the high level which is eighteen feet high, and a quar- ter of an hour later he was found lying on the ground in an unconscious state. As there is a two- railed fence three feet high protecting the high level, it appeared impossible to suggest how he had fallen. He was taken to the hospital and attended by Dr. McCambridge, but he died on Tuesday from' fracture of the skull. The evidence showed that although the man was not drunk, he had had in- toxicating liquor. A verdict of " Accidental death" was returned and the jury added a presentment that foremen of works should not allow a man to commence wozk who was under the influence of drink.

div.head: CHRISTMASTIDE AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: CHRISTMASTIDE AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

The revolution of time has brought another Christmas, and for once in a way the weather is typical of the season. A severe frost has prevailed for over a week and although no snow has fallen, nature is covered with a white mantle and skaters are enjoying themselves on all the pits in the neigh- bourhood. The season of plenty of good cheer, the tradesmen on Wednesday made a special show of their wares and the streets were crowded with sightseers in the evening. The butchers and poul- terers attracted the most attention, people continu- ally crowding round the shops, to view the huge sides of beef, the woolley headed sheep and all varieties of the feathered tribe. The tailors and drapers and bootmakers also made their places of business as bright as possible and the grocers estab- lishments were visions of plenty. On Thursday the weather was very foggy all day, and always a busy time on the railway the work of the officials was doubly increased by this condition of the atmosphere. The traffic had to be conducted by means of fog signals and many of the trains were running two and three hours late. Fortunately no accidents are reported. Yesterday, Christmas day, the frost continued in all its sever- ity but the weather was much clearer and brighter and the Christmas festivities were carried on unin- terruptedly in adverse climatic conditions. In the moraing services were held at the churches and Catholic Chapels and special music was sung. In the evening tea parties were held in connection with several of the Nonconformist schools and at Run- corn Public Hall the Tonic Sol-fa choir rendered the Messiah, accompanied by an efficient orchestral band and the principals were Miss Lee, Miss Bow- mont and Messrs. Grimshaw and Maltby.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD SCHOOLS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD SCHOOLS.
PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.

- - The children attending' Greenway-road Board Schools separated for the Christmas holidays on Wednesday afternoon, but re-assembled in the evening when two entertainments were given and prizes were distributed to those scholars who had been most regular in their attendance. The girls were first entertained by a series of magic lantern views and then Dr. McDougall distributed prizes to 29 girls. Those who had made the bess attendance were E, Wright, E. Duncalf, B. Mellor, H. Cook, E. Weston, and A. Duncalf. Dr. McDougall ad- dressing the scholars afterwards, said he was very pleased to be present and to help in the good work that was being carried on in those schools. He hoped they would profit by the lessons they were taught and culti- vate habits of industry and thrift, and always tell the truth, so that when they grew up to womrnhood they would be useful members of: the community. He wis glad to say that for these entertainments and prizes not one penny was charged to any per- son who was not a voluntary contributor—that was to say that not one penny came from the rates. The whole of the credit was due to the teachers,who in their laudable efforts to get the children to attend school re- gularly, helped those who could not help themselves. He had great pleasure in distributing the prizes and conse- quently encoura,7ing the teachers and staff of the school in the excellent work in which they were engaged. He hoped that in future years prizes would not only be given for regular attendance but for distinction in the classes. In this vray each child's character and ability would be brought out much more prominently than hail hitherto been the case. In conclusion he wished them all a merry Christmas and a happy and prosperous New Year. (Applause.)—Mr. Moulton said he and the other teachers were much obliged to Dr. McDougall for the suggestion he had made, and he thought the scholars might look forward next year to having prizes distri- buted for success at the examination in addition to prizes for regular attendance. He was sure all present were indebted to Dr. McDougall foe his presence and support. (Applause.) As the girl left the room an orange was presented to each. The room was then quickly filled with the boys, who had been waiting outside.—Mr. James Pritchard, chairman of the Board, before distributing the prizes, delivered a brief speech in which he said there were a few boys who had not been absent from school oa one single occasion sinee last January, and their names were :—William Barker, John Hughes, Walter Ellis, Ernest Moores:Frank Barton, Thomas Darlington, and Alfred Bentley. The following boys had not been absent once since mid- summer :—Wilfrid Dutton, George Whitlow, Richard Bate, James Moss, Walter Lewis, William Whitlow. Prizes would be distributed to these boys and also to those who had only been away three times in the half year. Altogether he would have to distribute 60 prizes and such results of regular attendance were a great credit to the school. Regular attendance was a very important matter without which there could not be efficient teaching or a successful school, and he was glad to find such a satisfactory attendance and that they were making such progress.. He had no doubt the prizes would be much appreciated and as a result he trusted they would render every help to their teachers that they would endeavour to seek the welfare of the schools at large. He. agreed with pr. McDougall's suggestion as to giving prizes for success in class work, and went on to explain, that the funds for prizes had been received from entertainments given from time to time during the past twelve months. It was particularly kind of Mr.Kynnersley,the inspector of that district, to come to give them a lecture, from which the handsome sum of £5 was realised. Not one penny had come from the rates, and the prizes were owing entirely to the energetic efforts and resources of the teachers. He trusted more scholars would receive more prizes next year, and he wished them all a happy Christmas and New Year. (Applause.) Mr. Moulton expressed the thanks of the teachers to Mr. Pritchard for distributing the prizes, A magic lantern entertainment was then given,

Several persons have been frozen to death in various parts of France. At the congregation at Cambridge on Wednesday the election of a chancellor in place of the Duke of Devon- shire was fixed for January 4th. Among those men- tioned as probable candidates for the office are the Prince of Wales, Duke of Rutland, Lord Hartington, and Lord Derby.

WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. The usual meeting of this society was held in the school- room on Monday evening, Mr. Brereton in the chair. A very interesting paper on "Iron " was read by Mr. Thos. Chorley. FOOTBALL.—A match was played at Lymm, on Satur- day, between Lymm Association and Manchester Corin- thians. Half time arrived with the score at nil, but at the end of the match the score was—Lymm, three goals; Corinthians, nil. Thomason,Henshaw, Weave and Holt played well for Lymm. • ENTERTAINMENT AT THE GR.AMMAR SCHOOL.—An enter- tainment was given at the Grammar School, on Monday evening. The programme was very well gone through, add consisted of violin and pianoforte solos, trios, quar- tettes, a French play, a farce, Sze. Among those who took part in the proceedings were Mr. Sowerbutts, sen., Mr. Sowerbutts, pin., Mr. McGill, Mr. Edwin Ferris,Miss McGill, and some of the pupils. The entertainment closed with the singing of the National Anthem.

THE GLASS INDUSTRY OF ST. HELENS,

MEETING FOREIGN COMPETITION, The plate-glass manufactuters of St. Helens, are engaged in making arrangements for carrying out improvements and alterations in their works which are expected to bring about almost a revolution in the manufacture of plate-glass locally, and have an influence which will be felt in the plate-glass markets of the world. These proposed alterations and improvements, principally iniregard to the ma- chinery, will be so vast and extensive that the total estimated cost is nearly £300,000, and the work will necessitate three or four years' continuous labour. Inquiries have elicited that these steps are not being taken by any individual firm, but the adoption of the best and newest machinery is forced upon the English manufacturers by the keen com- petition which they have to encounter from the foreign makers, principally those of France and Belgium. For many years the St. Helens, or "English," plate- glass manufacturers have undoubtedly been pre-eminent in the markets of the world, and in the quality of the material, as well as its price, have thoroughly beaten their foreign rivals. But, it is stated, they are now ex- periencing a keener competition than at any previous period in the history of the trade. It was explained that the present position of affairs had arisen from the fact that the St. Helens firms had been content with the sup- itmaey woo ',ears ago, and had continued to work with machinery and processes then adopted, which, at the time, were beyond a doubt the best and most complete that money could purchase. But during the last few years the Belgian makers have been putting down new plant, and adopting improvement after im- provement until the necessity has been forced upon the home manufacturers of practically recon- structing many portions of their works, if they are to maintain their well-earned position at the head of the world's plate-glass industry. This necessity, will not be shirked by the English glassmakers as represented by St. Helens firms, Though the outlay upon the alter- ations will amount to hundreds of thousands of pounds, and though years will pass before they are finally corn - pleted, the three great plate glass making firms of St. Helens, namely the London and Manchester Company, Messrs. Pilkington Bros., and the Union Plate-glass Company, have all determined to carry out the necess- ary changes., It has been found on inquiry that the three local firms are not carrying out the new works by any pre-arrange- ments ; but recently expired patents and all the latest known improvements are being brought into use in- dividually in order to maintain the acknowledged sup- eriority of British plate-glass over that of foreign manu- facture. It is, however, considered to be a singular coincidence that the keen competition from abroad should have forced the local manufacturers to adopt such extensive measures of self-preservation practically at the same moment. At each of the works of the three firms named the improvements will have the object of effecting not enly an immense saving of time and labour but a great reduction in the cost of production. Up to the present time the processes known as "grind- ing, "smoothing," and " polishing" of plate-glass while in course of manufacture have been carried out in separate departments and have required separate machinery. These operations have occupied a period of about three days, with all the attendant difficulties and losses arising from breakages in the transporting of the plates from one department to another. The new plant •to be introduced, however, is to bring about some re- markable changes. It is stated that the whole of the "grinding," smoothing, and polishing will be accom- pliahed by the same machinery:; that there will be no necessity for the removal of the plates, as under present conditions, and that instead of the operations taking up a period of three days, the whole of the work will be finished in one day. If these results are achieved their ultimate affect on the local plate-glass industry cannot at present be foreseen. The intre,l action of the new plant is not expected to interfere' any great extent with the employes of the firms cb xerned, The machinery will be introduced gradually. so as to prevent any stoppage of the works.. The well-known firm of Messrs. Pilkington Brothers appear to have been the first in the field locallj for the adoption of the new plant. It is known that for many months past, and particularly during the recent strike at their Cowley Hill Glassworks, the employers have had men at work carrying out necessary alterations or addi- tions preparing for the new appliances. It is stated that the firm have purchased the exclusive rights for the use of what is known as the Mervienx plant in this country, and some months ago engaged the services of a French expert to teach their workmen the principles of the new process of manufactute. The firm of Messrs. Pilkington Bros. commenced operations in 1827, and it is under- stood that at present they employ about 1,600 hands in the making of plateglass. The estimated outlay by Messrs. Pilkington Bros. in connection with the new plant could not be ascertained, but it is understood to amount to many thousands of pounds. The directors of the London and Manchester Plate-glass Company have had the matter of foreign oompetttion under consideration of some months, and the result of their deliberations was made known last week, when a prospectus was issued for mortgage debentures to the ameunt of 05,000, being the first portion of an issue of debentures limited to £200,000. It was stated that the debentures were issued in view of extensive alterations, additions, and reconstructions, and the introduction of new and improved machinery in the company's works. No details of these proposed works were given, but in- quiries elicited the fact they would be to the effect al- ready indicated. It is stated that the alterations and reconstructions would be commenced at once, and would not be finally completed for four or five years. The pre- sent works of the company comprise two vast establish- ments, one at Ravenhead, and the other at Sutton, both of which are devoted wholly to the manufacture of plate glass. The works at Ravenhead are of historical interest, as being the first plate-glass works erected in the king- dom. The first company for the manufacture of British plate glass was incorporated in 1773, and commenced operations at Ravenhead, but they were not successful in then. first venture, and in 1798 the concern was trans- ferred to a new company—the British Plate-glass Com- pany. The new management had a success beyond the highest expectation, and brought about a general ack- nowledgment that British plate glass was superior to that of any other country. The present London and Manchester Plate-glass Company commenced operations

at Sutton in 1836, and opened what are now known as the extension works in 1868. In that year, too, they became the lessees of the Ravenhead works, and the company is now stated to be the largest firm of plate- glass manufacturers in the kingdom, and are only ex- ceeded in the whole world by the St. Gobain Plate-glass Company in France. Nearly 1,800 hands are found em- ployment, including 1,200 men, 200 women, and about 350 young persons. The Union Plats-glass Company's works are situated at Parr' and it is stated that the firm a week or two ago decided to expend £20,000 in introducing new plant and making necessary alterations. Some hundreds of men are employed, and it is understood that the intended im- provements will not necessitate the stoppage of any of the hands.

BETWEEN TWO FIRES.

On Saturday Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Griffin Hotel, Peasley Cross, touching the death of John Ashcroft, 25 years of age, of 41, Iturtonhead-road, a collier, who died at the Cottage Hospital, on the previous Thursday, from injuries received on the Bth inst. in the Peas- ley Cross Collieries. Mr. H. Hall, Government in- spector, attended the inquiry. Before the jury were sworn, the deputy-coroner said he understood that one of the jurymen had something to say to him.— Mr. Thomas Leigh (juror) : I wish to say, sir,that I have been summoned here,and I have had to close my master's place of business in order to attend. I have no one yonder to take my place, and my em- ployer says that I can take my choice of instant dis- missal or attend to his business.—The Deputy Coroner: Who is your employer? Mr. Leigh : William Henry Gordon.—The Deputy Coroner : Is he a resident in this neighbourhood? Mr. Leigh : Yes, but he has had to go out on business.—The Deputy Coroner: Do you know whether he has ever been on a jury? Mr. Leigh : Yell% many a time.—The Deputy Coroner: Well, per- haps we had better have him here again.—Mr. Leigh: It Is Saturday morning, and it is very awkward for rue.— The Deputy Coroner: Yes, and very awkward for every gentleman. You are not the only shopkeeper. If your master had sent a civil sort of message that it was put- ting him to a great inconvenience we could have listened to. him, but not when he talks of instant dis- missal. I am inclined to treat a man with con- tempt who would threaten a valuable servant like you with instant dismissal because you are asked to come here and assist in getting through this short in- quiry. I would suggest that you say no more about it, but sit down and consent to be sworn. If you don't— and I am not going to force you—the only alternative is for me to fine you.—Mr. Leigh: I understand a'' about the alternative, but that has nothing to do with him. It is simply a question with me of neglecting his business. He said, if I neglected his business he would discharge me.—The Deputy Coroner: You are not neg- lecting your business in attending to that of the Queea. —Mr. Leigh: But the shop is closed, and people cannot get in.—The Deputy C3roner : I am afraid the people must wait. You are here and must be sworn. If you will not you will be fined. The rest of the jury are hert, and we will try to keep you as short a time as possible. I don't want to prolong the inquiry, and I don't think anybody else does.—The jury were then sworn and the inquiry proceeded. It appeared that deceased and other men were returning along one of the pit tunnels while some waggons were in motion. The men got in a man- hole, but a waggon left the road and caught the deceased, who Was fatally crushed. It was contrary to the regu- lations for men to walk along the tunnels while the wag- gons were in motion, and the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," adding that it was due to the im- prudence of the deceased and his companions.

The Bishop of Sodor and Man has been translated to the See of Carlisle. Lord Russell read the lessons at St. John's Church, Winchester, on Sunday night. Mr. Edward Langtry (husband of Mrs. Langtry) was on Monday installed Master of the Menai Bridge Masonic Lodge. The Guion Steamship Company's screw steamer Abys- sinia, which left New York for Liverpool on the 13th inst., has been burnt at sea. All hands, however, were saved. Moscow Bumbles don't like interference. Owing to his attempt to suppress corruption in the Municipal Council, the Grand Duke Sergius was hissed at an enter- tainment.

div.head: COURSING AT VirARBURTON,
div.p: COURSING AT VirARBURTON,

The B.ealley and Warburton Coursing meeting was held on Saturday. Some extremely good run- ning was witnessed, as the hares were very wild on account of the recent severe weather, giving the dogs much difficulty before they succeeded in catch- ing them. The judge was Mr. J. Cope, and the slipper Mr. T. Wilkinson. CONCERT AT GREAT SA.NKEY BOARD SCHOOL. On Monday evening a concert was given in the Board Schools, Great Sankey, by the school children, under the conductorship of Mr. George Clarke, the schoolmaster. The object of the concert was to raise funds to provide the scholars with a tea party, &c., consequently there was a good attendance of parents and friends. Two members of the School Bcard, Messrs. W. P. Skelton (vice-chairman) and the Rev. E. S. Jackson, were also present. The pro- gramme consisted of choruses, songs, glees, and a piccolo solo. The choruses and glees were all selected from the operas of the present day. Mr. J. Parkinson accompanied the pieces on the organ, in an able manner. The songs, &c., in the progamme were given by the following Wilding, Miss E. Moss, Miss A. M. Boardman, M. Longshaw, J. Melling, Miss S. Moss, Miss O. Cooke, Master J. Bingham. The two songs in the second part of the programme by Master Wilding were given in nigger costume, and were much appreciated causing con- siderable amusement. The songs, &c., in the pro- gramme were frequently interspersed with choruses and glees by the Children. Daring the interval in the programme, the prizes were presented to the scholars by Mr. W. P. Skelton. Two certificates for drawing were given to J. Melling and E. Davies, also Melling was presented by the Board with a box of colours for general excellence in his studies. At the conclusion of the programme, Mr. Jacluon prcposed, and put to the meeting that a very hearty vote of thanks be accorded to Mr. Clarke, Mr. Par- kinson, the performers, and Mr. Skelton, for the services they had rendered, which was carried with applause.—Mr. Clarke replied on behalf of himself and the children, and Mr. Skelton also replied.

div.head: GHOST
div.p: THE GHOST
HUNTHORPE HALL
BY MRS. CHARLES MATTHEWS.

"Where 'do you spend Christmas, Jack? " asked Oliver Conway of his friend, as they met at the Club, shortly before the 25th. " ith the Suttons, ut Ilunthorpe." "De you? That is good news, I am going there. too ; but I thought you had not seen much of them lately, in fact I fancied that prettycousin of Dick's had—" 4'4 You thought that Margery Artnaro had refused tee, you mean? No it never came en that, because never was able to screw up courage to ask her. the does not live with the &Atolls now, you knew, tsince her father, told Sir John, came back from India %he has been with him, at their place in Lincoln- shire, and Dick tells me she is'quite devotedlo the .old man, whey by the way, is the most hot-tem- Vered, pig-headed old gentleman you ever saw. If :he once gets hold of an idea, nothing can move him, and now, it seems, he has set his heart on,marrying .Margery te that fellow .Lawford, simply because 'the properties join. However, I don't know that it is of much consequence, for I don't believe that Margery cares a straw for me. The only time I &saw her in London she scarcely spoke to me."

" Wellony dear fellow, perhaps she was piqued at your neglect. You can't expect a girl to be very demonstrative to a man who knows she is in town and does not go near her.for weeks." "I wish I could think so, however Dick knows how the matter stands, and has asked me down for 'Christmas, because she will he,there, and I can't makeup my mind to refuse." "What sort of a place is Hunthorpe Hall 2 " "I don't know, I have not seen it yet. They lbave only lately tau). it. When do you go down?" "On the,23rd, by the express." "So do I, so we shall meet at the station.' "Yes, good-bye, till then. Keep up a good heart, • old fellow. You don't know what luck may be in store for you." It was bitterly cold, old-fashioned snowy Christ- mas weather, when the friends met at the station. .As they hurried along in search of a smoking car- riage, something in the lines of a profile seen dimly through the frosty glass of a window caused Jack •to turn and look again, and to his surprise and delight he recognised the face which was occupying all his thoughts and dreams. He flung away his cigar, and calling hastily to Conway that he would get in here, he opened the carriage door and took his seat opposite its only occupant, just as the train Moved out of the station. There was a very pretty flush on Margery's cheeks and an unwonted light in her eyes, as she recognised the frank handsome • face of Jack Graham; and when, after an hour's - van the train stopped for the first time and Oliver • wane to see what had become of his friend, he found _ _ _ .

film apparently much improved in health and spirits and altogether quite a different person from the love-lorn swain he had known of late, and Conway returned to his cigar and paper, much relieved as to his friend's condition, and full of thankfulness, that hitherto he had contrived to avoid the ups and &awns of the tender passion. It had ceased snowing, but the clouds still lay dark and heavy on the horizon, with one faint yellow gleam where the pale sun was setting, when they arrived at Hunthorpe-station, and found the Sutton's dog-cart waiting for them. Conway generously took the back seat, and Jack having seen that Margery was well protected from the chill air, took the reins, and they set off at a brisk trot over the frozen snow and soon reached the gate, beyond which the drive swept through a thick plantation to the house. As far as they could see in the dusk, Hunthoue Hall was a long rambling building of red-brick, the iglu line broken by numerous quaint gables and curiously twisted chimneys. The bare branches of the gnarled oaks which surrounded the house, looked in the dim light, like the writhing limbs of tortured giants, and the last faint light of the dying day was reflected from the deep pool encircled by a belt of fir trees which lay to the kft. A blaze of light and warmth greeted the travellers az the door opened, and Mrs. Sutton and Dick ran out on to the steps and welcomed them, as guests are welcomed at Christmas time only. And there was no doubt as to the season when they entered, for holly and ivy and mistletoe almost covered the black oak panels of the large hall, while a goodly yule log flamed and crackled in the wide chimney, and lighted up the bright dresses of the party gathered around it. There were laughing greetings and introductions, and the new corners were speedly installed in the warmest corners. So your father could not come with you, Mar- gery ? ' said Mrs. Sutto "No, he w'aa-olDliged to gTirrown this evening, and as I was determind not to lose a day of this merry-making, I persuaded him to let me come on alone." "And you met Jack and Mr. Conway at the station, that was very fortunate, and all came down together." None of the three seemed to consider it necessary to mention that Conway had preferred his cigar to his friends' company, and the subject dropped. At dinner jack contrived to sit next to Margery, and made such good use of his opportunity, that when the party separated shortly before midnight, he was so delighted with the result that he felt in a most arnia.ble and Christmas-like frame of mind towards all the world, including even "that fellow Lawford," who, to do him justice had not attempted to interfere with him, being corn. pletely occupied with Dick's lively little sister Nelly. As the men drew near the fire in the smoking- room, Dick looked round with a beaming smile and exclaimed, "Its awfully jolly to see you here old fellows, and very good of you all to come such a distance to a tumbledown old place like this." " Tumbledown ! It's perfectly delightful," said Jack, who saw everything couleur de rose. " Ah, you've only seen it lighted up and full of people. How mother and Nelly can stand it when they are alone, I can't imagine, but they took a fancy to the place directly they saw it, and I eouldn't persuade them to give it up. Then it was in a fearful state of decay, but mother has spent no end of money on it, and it would be too hard on her if she was obliged to leave it now." "Why should she leave it ?" "Well, Isecause, because— I may as well make a clean breast of it at once, the fact is the ser.7ants have all sivea rotios in a body; because they say the house is nauirted." "Of course," said Conway," They always do in the country, it's a regular dodge to get higher wages." "I am afraid it isn't that here, for nothing will bribe them to stay, it was only by promising to fill the house and leave no corners for ghosts, that we • could keep them over Christmas, besides which, my mother herself declares she has seen something." "Seen something ?" "What sort of a thing ?" ." What was it like ?" exclaimed a chorus of voices. "Well," said Dick, and they all drew their chairs closer round the fire "this is the tale. One evening when I was in town, my mother and Nelly were sitting in the drawing-room, John the old man servant came in, and asked if they had rung, my mother said no, and he went away. Shortly . after he appeared again, and stood at the door. My mother said, I did not ring John." Very odd, ma'am,' he replied, the bell certainly rang, and as he stood with the door open a bell rang dis- -tinctly somewhere. My mother went to the servants' hall, and found the household assembled In a group, gazing open-mouthed at the bells, and -while she was there one of them moved and rang unmistakeably, That is not the drawing-roombell,' •she said that belongs to the library. Now the library is still unfurnished, and has been kept locked ,since we came. My mother took a candle and went to the room. It was empty, quiet, and quite undisturbed. She sent Nelly to watch while she rang the bell. .It was that bell sure enough. She went back to the servants and tried to persuade them that rats must have got at the wires, but confesses that she convinced neither them nor her- self. She and Nelly were sitting up over the drawing-room fire, trying to invent explanations of the mystery, when they both heard the bell ring again, and the same moment they both saki hush 1' and listened, and the sound of wheels became louder and louder. It must be Dick come back unexpectedly," said Nelly, and ran into the hall. Don't open the door ' cried my mother, and hurried up to her dressing-room which overlooks the drive. She threw open the window and looked out. There before the door was a carriage and pair, and as far as she could sea in the darkness a figure seemed to be getting out. Is it you Dick?' she cried. No answer. At that moment the house bell rang loudly, she ran down to the hall, and down also came John, and she bade him open the door. This he did very cautiously. No one entered. They lcoked out. No one there. They took a light and examined the ground. No trace of wheels or horses. My mother passed the night in trying in vain to convince herself that the carriage was a phantom conjured up by her excited imagina- tion but could not get over the fact, that she and lad ilrard_the_sonnd of wheels at the eau.,

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 26, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 26, 1891.

moment. For the hell, theft waa the usual explanation—rats. In the morning she sent for the bell-honr.p.r, and explained, that she wanted the bells and the wires thoroughly •examined and put ia order. Certainly, I'll over 'au! 'ern ma'am,' said he, but it aint no manner of use, I've been over them wires eight or nine times, and "mows every turn and twist of ;ern. The fact is ma'am, the 'ouse is 'aunted, 'aunted as bad as 'ouse can be. Eight or nine families 'as tried it, but they always 'as to leave. The servants gets frightened, and gives notice in a body. 'Ave you seen the carriage, ma'am ?' he added. My mother confessed she thought she had. 'A carriage and pair warn't it ma'am? Yes, that's it sure enough. And in answer to her questions he told this story

Bak, and thsl iliof the" El-en at kit rea-Ched—ilie ' earsof the dancers, who flung open the door, rushed out, and the horses were at length quieted and is away. " Now then," mid Dick, for Lawford's prize," and heading a procession, he led the way to the smoking room. "flow is this ? " said he, "the key is on the outside." This appeared truly marvellous, till Lawford confessed he had dropped it in his attack. Dick opened the door and peeped cautiously in. Seated in an arm chair drawn cosily near the fire. his face glowing with the mingled effects of the cold air and the hot spirits, a glass of steaming punch on the little table beside him, and, close at hand, Jack Graham preparing a second potion, to Dick's utter astonishment he beheld his uncle' Sir John , Munro Bart, At first, amazement kept him dumb, but at length the humour of the affair over- came him, and he fairly screamed with laughter. "What the deuce is the meaning of this ?" thun- dered the old gentleman. "Is it not enough to have been dragged out of my own carriage by a set of young scoundrels, suffocated in my own rug, and shut up in a dark room, but I am to be made a laughing-stock and exhibition to a crowd of grinning idiots? What does it moan, sir, I ask again ?" "My dear John," said Mrs. Sutton, "what a dreadful mistake, I am so very sorry—* "The fact is, au.," said Conway, for a ghost." "Ghost, young num? Ghost, indeed! a pack of lies. Do I look like a ghost ?" He did not, in deed; his short, round form and rosy face had little affinity with the spirit world. There is only one gentleman amongst you," he went on, "and that is this young man," pointing t(Pjaok, who has had the good sense to keep aloof from such fooling, and sufficient kindness of heart to help a poor ill-used old man to pull himself to- gether." " Jack !" said Dick. "Why he was—" Jack made frantic signs from behind the old man's chair, and Conway promptly broke in and drowned the rest of Diek's speech. Mrs. Sutton at last prevailed on Sir John to accept the young men's apologies, though he sternly refused. to belief it to have been anything but a premeditated ioke ; and Margery took advantage of thefavourable impression produced by Jack's discreet conduct, and before the party broke up had ob- tained her father's consent to their marriage. Whether the rough treatment of the visitor reached the ears of the Spirits we do not know, but certain it is no more mysterious carriages were seen con- veying ghostly guests to Hunthorpe

"Many years ago Hunthorpe Hall belonged to a certain Sir Martin Redlaw, who in racing, gambling, and drinking had managed to squander a fine fortune. His only chance of keeping the old house lay in marrying his daughter Phcebe to a Squire Hervey, a neighbour, a „plan of the same type as himself, who held the irortgage on the estate. But Phoebe, it seems, was in love with her cousin Ralph, who. was abroad fight- ing for his country, and swore that as long as he lived she would marry no one else. Hervey contrived that false news 'of her cousin's death should reach Plumbe, and then heartbroken and caring little what became of her, she at last con- sented to marry Hervey, on condition tint they should live at the hall. A few months sufficed to weary Hervey of his coveted prize, and he returned to his old ways often leaving his wife for weeks together in the desolate house, for her father died shortly after her useless sacrifice. During one of these absences Ralph returned and learned what had happened. Almost mad with rage and grief he determined to meet his cousin, and hear from her own lips the reason of her desertion. Fearing she would refuse to see him, if he declared himself openly, he hung disguised about the village till Hervey left, and then by bribes and entreaties induced the old butler, who had known him from a child, to let him enter and find his way by a secret passage to the library where Phoebe always lived when alone; and on Christmas Eve as shesat sadly by the dying erribers thinking of Ralph, and of her wasted life, to her horror she saw the picture of Ralph's father which hung on the panel that served as entrance to the secret passage, slowly move and as she thought advance towards her. She gave a shriek of terror and seizing the bell rang violently, and sank fainting at the feet of her lover. While he was trying to restore her, he was startled by the sound of wheels and the peal of the house bell; immediately after, the door was flung open and Hrvey strode into the room calling loudly for his wife. On seeing her in the arms of his rival, he uttered a fearful oath, and calling her by every vile name, he dragged the half conscious girl to the door, and bidding her begone flung her from him with such violence that she fell, striking her head on the stone pavement of the hall, so that 'she lay quite dead. Ralph drew his sword, and springing on Hervey before he had time to defend himself, lie ran him through the body, shrieking liar 'and' murderer,' then rushed out into the darkness, and flung him- self into the deep pool in the fir wood; and the story runs that from time to time the bell in the library rings as if Phcebe were puffin,t' it in her mortal terror, and Hervey drives up as he did that night; and the man ended his tale by saying All the families that 'as been 'cre 'as always heard the bell and seen the carriage on Christmas Eve, if they aint before.'" They were all silent as Dick finished his story, but in a few moments explanations and conjectures came fast enough. "What do you think of the matter, Dick ?" asked Conway. "Do you believe in this luxurious ghost who keeps a carriage and pair for his own special convenience ?" "I hardly know what to think, old fellow. My own view is that the whole affair is got up by the farmer who lives here when the house is not let, and who much objected to turning out when we came, and I propose to stop his game in this way. To-morrow being Christmas Eve we may expect the ghost, and I intend, if two or three of you will help me, to lie in wait for it. A CHURCH which desired to get rid of an aged pastor who had long served it held a meeting to consider the matter. After considerable discussion one of the deacons who had hitherto said nothing, getting impatient, arose and said—" Mr. Cheerman, I move that Mr. H.'s usefulness in this 'ere field come to an eend arter to-night." The motion was carried. Churches sometimes bring a pastor's "usefulness to an end" without a formal vote. It is easily done when a few people set themselves to it.—Christian Inquirsr. A WEST of Scotland clergyman was going to the Highlands for his holidays, and being very fond of the "Nabob Pickles" he took a bottle with him. The "Nabob Pickles" are extremely hot, and should be sparingly used. Arrived at a hotel, he placed the bottle on the table, and took one or two of them. A Yankee was sitting opposite, and got his eye on the pickles. " Stranver, pass the pickles, please." The clergyman said—" These are private property, but you are welcome to them." He passed the bottle across the table. The Yankee emptied half the bottle into his plate, and stirred them well up with his spoon. He took a big spoonful, but they were sot long down when he drew a long breath and said, " Oh, dodirast it! Look here, stranger. I guess you are a parson ?" " Well, lam a clergy- man, and I preach the Gospel." "Look you here," said the Yankee, " I have heard them preach about Ere and brimstone, but you are the first one I know who carries a sample bottle." LANDLADY—" You cfin't tell me that you found no comfort in your bed last night, Mr. Newman." New Boarder (who found his bed quite hard)— "Well, if it was comfort, ma'am, it was pretty solid comfort.'
