*„. Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that sports of matches played ou Saturday must be sent to the ead office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten 'elock on Wednesday morning.

RUGBY. RUNCORN A v. LI/1310'001. OLD Boys A.—Played at Runcorn on Saturday. The home team started the game when the visitors defended their line strongly, until A. Tyler broke down the defence, May missing the goal kick. Resuming, the Old Boys got near the home line, when Henshaw had a dangerous shot at goal. Final score Runcorn, one goal and three tries, to Old Boys

nil. WIDNHS v. ST. HEILENS.—At Widneson Saturday. The home team kicked off uphill, but the visitors at once attacked, Cross and Joites scoring tries, which, however, were not improved, tlie score at half-time being in favour of St. Helens by 2 tries to nil. After the interval Widnes played much better, and Whelan scored, Brennan kicking a goal, thus giving the home team the lead. Final result—Widnes, 5 points ; St. Helens, 4
points. FRODSIZAM T. VIDNEs RAnsElßS.—Frodsliam journeyed

to Widnes with a weak team to meet the Rangers, on Saturday. From the start the visitors had the best of the play, pressing nearly the whole time. They crossed the line on several occasions, but the referee ruled in favour of the home team time after tithe, and at the end of the first half nothing was scored. After the restart Froisham had still the best of matters, and the home team did not once cross the half-way line. After the visitors had had four tries disallowed, F. Darlington, after a strong run, scored near touch. T. Darlington took the place, but failed to impnve, and Frodsham won by one try to nil. STOCKTON MUTE 2ND V. WARRINGTON RANGERS 2ND.— This match was played at Stockton Heath. on Saturday. The Rangers commenced, and the kick being charged down the homesters took the ball over the line, a minor resulting. The dron out found the homesters pressing, and after some tricky play Downs scored. Birchall mak- ing a good bid for goal. The visitors now tried hard to equalise,but could not break through the home defence; and at half time nothing further had been scored. The second portion of the game found the visitors mostly on the defensive, and after some neat passilig by the home backs, Barber eluded all his opponents, but slipped close to the line. Shortly afterward, however, Barber again got possession,and gained a splendid try near the corner ' flag,Birchall doing the needful. On resuming, however, the home forwards took the ball over the line, but lost possession, a minor resulting. Nothing further being scored, the call of time found the Heathens victors of a pleasant game by 1 goal, 1 try, 2 minors, to 1 minor. WA RRINOTON RANGERS v. SIIAMROCKS. Played at Warrington. The home captain lost the toss, and Whitfield started the game, by a cross kick to Eden who ran and kicked down the field, and Ashurst, taking up the running, scored a clever try a minute from the start, the samo player placing a goal. Massey had hard lines, after a grand run half the length of the field slip- ping when close to the line. Not to be denied,however, the homesters kept up the attack, and from loose play Ashurst got possession, and dropped a smart goal. Two goals ahead in less than ten minutes from the start was indeed a good performance, against such sturdy oppo- nents. The visitors,however, warmed up to their work, and Ryan receiving the ball effected a fine run, but the sure tackling of the Rangers prevented a score. The game was hotly contested, the home team showing vastly im- proved form. Half time arrived with the score Rangers 2 goals,2 minors,to Leigh one minor. During the second half both teams played with great dash, the strong for- ward bursts of the visitors being neutralised by the pas- sing and kicking of the Rangers' backs, who were play- ing splendidly. The game continued to be in favour of the home team, Whitfield scoring a clever try after a good run. The visitors were now completely over- played, Ashurst putting on a final touch by securing his second try and placing a goal. The game finally ended with the score Rangers 3 goals, I try, 3 minors to Leigh 1 minor. _ _ _

_ STOCKTON HEATH v. WARRINGTON ST. MARY'S. —On Saturday the Heathites paid St. Mary's a visit to try their first encounter with them. The homesters kicked off, and play soon became very lively about mid- field. From a scrimmage, however, the Saints broke away, forcing a minor. The drop-out found the homesters on the offensive, but Cross relieved to half way, and the visitors worked the ball to the home line, pressing the Saints for a time. From some loose play the home forwards got away, a minor resulting. The drop-out saw the play at half way where Rathbone obtained possession and passed neatly to Lawless, who transferred to Threadgold, the latter getting over, but the referee disallowed the point, owiseg to the ball having been grounded twice. The Heathites, however, were not to be denied,and Higham scored at the corner flag, Glover landing a goal. On resuming the visi- tors again pressed, having hard lines. At half-time Stockton Heath were leading by one goal. The visitors led off and soon pressed,and Hassall's kick being charged down, Morgan scored, no goal resulting. The Saints were now severely pressed, and Rathbone driobled the ball over the line, but had to wriggle his way through the spectators, and was robbed of an almost certain try. After the dropout Threadgold nearly got in after some neat passing. Owing ta some misunderstanding the homesters got into the visitors' quarters for the first time but nothing resulted, and on the call of time the Heath- ites ran out victors by one goal, one try, three minors ta, LVVU tninoro. WARRINGTON A v. MosseßY A.—This fixture was played on the Wilderspool ground, which was in bad condition, owing to the recent floods. Mossley started, and at once worked the leather into the home 25, Law- less and Lally, however, getting the ball well out of danger. Potts then grandly saved a rush of the visitors' forwards, and Thornley, Hampson, Phillips, and War- burton transferred the game to the Mossley end. For a time the combat waged 6 near midfield, until Lally and Lawless by kicks forced their opponents on the defen- sive. After Bailey had shown up, Lally made a grand run down the ground, scoring far out, Sampson making a good bid for goal. Immediately after the drop out Mossley got away, and the home backs mulling, Hibbs succeeded in equalizing. Dropping out, Lawless made a short run, but Mossley, by strong play, caused Warring- ton to defend, and after the home team had experienced an anxious few minutes, Taylor, from along throw out, got a smart try, Hibbs placing an easy goal. Having this advantage, Mossley adopted a style of play detri- mental to the open game; but after a series of packs Davies, Rowlands, Foster, and Russell finally broke through to the line. Roberts effected a good relief, but Hamblett, by a run and kick, made matters warm for visitors, who defended extremely well. Lawless then stopped Taylor in fine style, and Lally, Bailey, and Hampson were notable in their endaavours to force the ball over the line. A mull allowed the visitors to clear, but Sampson and Lawless replied splendidly. Mossley- , were now severely pressed, and Thornley, Davies, Hamp- son, and Warburton dribbled to the line. Mellor tem- porarily staved off disaster, but a punt by Lally returned the oval to the goal, and trom a rush Phillips scored, Sampson placing a good goal. Offside by Warrington lost a lot of ground, but Lawless racing round passed to Potts, who took the warfare to centre. Exchange kicks followed, and after Potts had put in a dashing piece of work, Roberts following his kick tackled Ham- blett in his 25. Hampson, Forster, Russell, and Phillips regained the lost ground, Sampson supplementing this by a foe punt. A kick by Mellor changed the scene of operations, and a kick being charged, Mossley got to the line, and from a smart pass Taylor dropped a goal, half- time arriving, Warrington 1-1-0 to 2-1-0. Upon the resumption of hostilitics Lawless put in a long kick, and Pickford being finely tackled, play settled down in the Mossley territory. A capital bit of play by Sampson caused the leather to be taken under the posts, but Lees relieved, and twice over saved splendidly. Hampson then dribbled to the visitors' citadel, but the danger was averted. Lawless, Davies, Rowlands, and Thornley were the means of pressure being again brought to bear on their opponents, and packs followed with monotonous regularity, until a minor was ',conceded. A grand run by Davies was succeeded by Lally scoring the second try. Good kicking by Sampson, in response to Taylor, ended in Forster, Warburton. Bailey, ;and Russell carrying the warfare to the visiting quarters, where Mossley showed good saving qualities, and after some desultory play Lawless secured possession, dodged round a scrimmage, and obtained a capital try under the posts, which Samp- on converted. No sooner had the game been started than Hampson, Phillips, and Thornley dashed down the ground, and Davies breaking away, punted the leather over the line, another minor given. beim?' Mossley then had a brief look in, but Potts, Russell, and Sampson nullified the effort, and an interesting game ended— Warrington 2-2-2 to Mossley 2-1-0. OLD BOYS V. RUNCORN.

Played at Fairfield before a good attendance. The sides were not at their full strength, Houghton, Riley, Evans, and Williams being among the absentees on the Runcorn side, while Russell and H. C. Wood stood out of the Boys' ranks. O'Dwyer opened the play, and the early passages were contested in the Runcorn half. Passing among the home backs took place,. but the leather was sent into touch, and ,frorn the line-out the visitors' front line broke away and registered a dead ball. Following the drop-out, Abrams picked up smartly and parted to Crompton, who in turn sent on to Davies, and the first try was registered near the corner flag, the nlace kick failing. After the drop out the play was evenly contested about midfield, when Harrison started a passing movement which threatened disaster to the Runcornians, but the forwards carried the packs, and the venue was as quickly changed. Here Abrams got possession, and ran nicely down, and timely passing to Shaw resulted in a second try, but the kick at goal was a failure. For the next few minutes the boys fairly held the play, but could not break through, and the interval arrived with the score in favour of Runcorn by four points to nil. The second half opened evenly, and some capital passing was witnessed between O'Dwyer, Wood, and Male, but it failed to bring about the desired result, andtDavies removed the scene to the other end. Cromp- ton made an effort to break through, but packs were formed,and Wilson and Bullen were mainly instrumental in saving the line, and on O'Dwyer sending out to Male, the latter player parted to the centre, who after a magnificent run, planted the ball behind the lit e, and successfully kicked the goal. From this point the game

was hotly contested, but neither side added to their score, and the Old Boys carried off the match by a goal to 2 tries or five points to four. Teams :—Old Boys.— J. Goold, back; W. H. Male, H. D. Wood, and W. H. Legge, three-quarter backs; J. B. O'Dwyer, and A. R. Harrison half-backs ; R. P. Wilson, E. W. &Alen, F. W. Henstock, J. Smellie, R. L. Armour, D. Nicol, W. Wat- son, R. M'Turk, and J. J. S. Rowe, forwards. Runcorn —Woods, back; T. Davies, Crompton, and Pendlebury, three-quarter backs ; Abrams and Robinson, half-backs; Faulkner, Hampson, Reece, Hughes, Massey, Webb, J. Davies, Stubs, and Shaw, forwards.
WARRINGTON v. MOSSLEY.

Warrington journeyed to Mossley, on Saturday, with an excellent combination, and as a result they succeeded in defeating the Mossleyites by three goals (fourteen points) to a try (to points). This is the first time the Warringtonians have ever defeated the Mossley Club on the Heights of Luzley, and that they well deserved their victory on Saturday is without doubt, for their play was brilliant throughout. The homesters had also mustered a capital 15, and the weather being of an agreeable description, there was no wonder at a fair" gate," tak- ing into consideration the poor support which has been extended to the" hilly youths.."

Warrington having- won the choice of ends, played with the slope, and Rowan's kick off being followed by Evans placing his side on the aggressive, Morrell had an anxious time of it in the first minute. Ogden was next at fault for Mossley, and Donohue was all but in, the saving tactics of Eagland spoiling the chance. Relief was forthcoming whea. Mossley were afforded a free kick and although this was the means of rushing the oval to Warrington quarters, the attack was but a mere flash- in-the-pan, for some neat exchanges between James and John Bate found Evans running strongly down touch, and finally kicking to Morrell, the latter being safely held in close proximity to his posts. Twice over the visiting forwards almost landed the ball over the line, Turner, Ashton, and Jolley being the prominent parties ; but Eagland eventually relieved to the quarter flag. Now was the Warrington's chance, and from a scrimmage near the quarter flag, James Bate passed across to his namesake, and the latter throwing to Heesom this player made no mistake, for handing the oval to Webster, the latter took the chance in true style, but being bordered on touch, he steadied himself and shot over the line near the posts for a brilliant try. Heesom placed the easy goal. The restart was met by Heesom, and a forward movement by Jolley, Ashton, Barnes and Berry again threatened the lower goal. It was left to Webster again to effect the downfall of the home citadel, for, receiving a neat pass from Heesom, he dropped a fine goal, thus giving his side the substantial lead of nine points. The last major point had an effect on the homesteads, and whereas they had mainly relied on the backs to save their lines, their forwards now put their shoulders to the " wheel" with good results. The brothers Corscadden and Newby headed a long dribble to the Warrington lines, and Boscow, who had been acting the part of spectator, was called so save his charge. Needless to say he was not found wanting, and a grand display between the Bates and Evans was supplemented by a combined effort by John Bate, Turner, Donohue, and Knowles. Evans was held on the line a moment later, whilst Heesom, after failing to take a pass, dribbled to Morrell for the latter to clear. Again the homesters reached half-way, and Boscow and Turner kicking judiciously, the latter charged Eagland's kick, but again the Mossley goal escaped. A short rush by the home forwards was saved by Evans in true style, and when everything had pointed to Mossley at last gaining a tangible score, Boscow appeared on the scene with a lofty kick, and the game was carried on at the Mossley end, Ashton and Berry dribbled finely, and than both of the visitors' half backs were within an acre of scoring. Webster next ran across and passed to Evans, the latter having a shot for goal, the kick realizing the first minor. The visitors. maintainarathe supremacy, and a marked contrast was noticeable in the two teams, for whereas one:was rather,loose in:their style, combina- tion which had been effective was noticeable on the

Warrington side. James Bate got in a fine run, but his pass to Evans,was a shade too high, but another move- ment, originating from the half backs still harrassed Morrell's charge. Some ,briiliant play by Ashton and Turner resulted in Berry scoring an easy try, and Heesom placed the third goal, this latter point bringing half-time, with the score as—Warrington, 3-0-1 ; Mossley, nil. With the lead of fourteen points to nil, :matters had anything but a rosy aspect for Mossley, but judging from their attack in the first few minutes they certainly thought themselves capable of the task set them. The Warrington backs were in„fine form, ;Boscow especially so, whilst Evans tackled with all his old skill. Eaglanil showed early promise by punting finely to Webster, but the latter was not found wanting, and a long dribble in which Jolley, Molyneux, Ashton, and Rauoies were the leading operators, found the game at the top of the in- cline. A long kick by Eaglancl at once changed the venue and a penalty kick falling to Warrington, Turner kept the line clear. Webster saved a minute later. The drop-out saw play at neutral ground, and a spell of passing by the Bates, Heesom, and Evans realized the Mossley 25. The Warrington backs were playing in fine form, Webster kicking finely on the popular side, and rarely missing finding touch. Eagland again caused his side to attack, and a fair catch by the same player was responded to by Boscow. James Bate and Webster passed and re- passed_alanalhp nonular side, and being backed up:bv some sterling torward-PPTY-1.-y-aQuaku„ltandles, and Turner, the Mossley goal was threatened. Eaglaud was the saviour of his side, and Taylor had a fine chance

from the Huddersfield man, but he had not calculated Evans' tackling qualities, for falling into this player's grasp he was soon floored, and Mossley were again dis- appointed. The visiting backs again passed well, but the effort was neutralised when Nield ran to the line and passed to Taylor for the latter to complete a neat try. This was M3ssley's last chance, for Warrington now pressed them severely, and runs by Turner and James Bate were deserving of better results. Only one minor was notched, aud a grand game was brought to a conclusion with the score as stated above.

Teams :—Warrington: Boscow, back; Evans, Web- ster, and Heesom, three-quarters; James and John Bate, half-backs; Turner, Ashton, Randles,Jolley,Berry, Donohue, Knowles,Molyneaux,and A. Barnes, forwards. Mossley : Morrell, back ; Taylor, Eagland, and Varley, three-quarters; Ogden and Neild, half backs; Batley, Bowers, Cunningham, J. and A. div.head: TWO CARTERS.
div.p: THE TWO CARTERS.

Rey. Samuel Carter was an easy-going, open. hearted, but terribly lazy preacher, who had been ' for many years settled over the old rree-Will Baptist Society, at Buttermilk Hollow. One day in early spring our good clergyman was on the road in his •old yellow gig, when he came across a poor carter, whose heavy cart, with a load of oak wook, had got stuok in the deep mud. The poor man was punching away at his oxen with his bradded goad-stick, when the parson came up. Now the carter's oxen were far from being over- fed. In fact, the sharp lines of their ribs would seem to indicate that they 'lacked food. The parson saw this, and thought fa administer a gentle reminder. "My good friend, you seem to be in trouble," he said, as he reined up alongside the cart. "I should say I was. I'm stuck here in the mud, like death to a dead hoss ! and I don't see how I'm goin' to get out." "My good man,—your oxen are too weak for such a load. Ah 1 You should be more care- ful of them. A humane man is humane to his beast."
"No ! You don't hit the case, mister. 'Taint the oxen that's in the fault. The trouble aint wi' them." _ _

"Why," returned the man of the cart, looking up as though he did not recognize the clergyman, his bleared eyes blinking sharply the while, "them poor oxen is like the Free-Will Baptist Society over in Buttermilk Holler,—they want to better Carter 1" _
After which the minister rode on, meditatively.

div.head: SAXE AND THE TIPSY GRENADIER.
div.p: SAXE AND THE TIPSY GRENADIER.
BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
HE KNEW THE COMMANDMENTS.

A lad, named Robert Pownall, aged nine years, was on Tuesday, charged before Messrs. R. Garnett and W. Owen, at the Warrington Police Court with having stolen 3s. 6d. in money, the property of John Lyons, clogger, Brick-st. The lad had gone to Lyons's workshop to buy a pair of tips and while there he took the 3s. 6d. from a drawer. On the money being missed suspicion rested upon the lad, and he was afterwards found with is. 81d. in his possession. He confessed to the theft and said he had given another lad is. He also spent some of the money on chocolate and "jaggy nuggets." The lad to whom be had aiven the shilling took the money home to his mother, and his mother took it back to Pownall's parents. Questioned by Mr. Garnett, the lad said he knew there were ten Commandments and one of them against stealing. The case was dismissed, on the lad's father promising to administer a judious punishment.

MARGARINE PROSECUTIONS. At the Warrington borough police court on Monday, Ellen Smith, Mersey-street, was charged by Inspector Norman with exposing margarine for sale on the 24th ult., properly labelled, and was fined 10s. and costs, 19s. in all.—Charles Baker, Fenn-11-street, was charged by Mr. Norman with the like offence on the same date, also with selling to him on that date margarine not properly labelled. Mr. Norman stated in his evidence that while he was in the shop the defendant sent a lad to his other shop in Church-street, to get the labels put on there before witness came,and the lad just got there as he did. A case as to the shop would be brought on another day. Mr. Norman said he was supplied with a pound of margarine at 10d. from a quantity which was marked pure butter. When he told him he meant to submit it for analysis he told him it was margarine. The defend- ant wanted to give him something, to say nothing about the matter.—The defendant denied this, and said he simply asked him if there was any way of paying a fine witl- out going to court, and Mr. Norman told him he had better see the Sanitary Committee. The defendant said the label which Mr. Norman mentioned was that of pure butter, which he had been selling just before the Inspec- tor came in.—Alderman Harrison, who was presiding during this case, characterised it as the worst he had heard in that court, and the defendant was fined 20s. and costs in each case, £2 Bs. in all.

It was stated that he had got into his father's house and assaulted him and broken several articlos. The father produced in court a poker which he said his son had used. The defendant was fined ss. and costs.—James Bird, drunk and dis- orderly in Bridge-st. on Sunday night, who had had to be put out of the Roebuck Inn, ss.—Kate Gunston, in Buttermarket-st., on the 14th inst., 55. UNSEEMLY LANGUAGEL—WiIIiam Finch, George Flan- naghan, and Michael McDonald, were charged with com- mitting this offence in Bridge-st., on the 13th inst. Finch was fined 10s. and costs and the others had to pay ss. and costs each. OBSTRUC mg.—John Musgrove, a youth, for obstruct- ing free passage in Leonard-st. by driving a pony .and cart on to the footpath, and who pleaded that the pony got on to it through shying at some water, was fined 55., including costs. FIGHTING.—George and James Hopkin and John and Martin Burke were charrd with fighting on Town Hill. Both the Hopkinses were sent t) jail for a month. John Burke was fined the costs, and Martin was dis- missed.
THURSDAY.—Before Captain Ridgway (chairman), and

Mr. John Fairciouah: DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John and Thomae Casey,in Parker-st., the previous night, ss. and costs each. CHARGES OF DESERTION.—Henry Grace,a Dallam forge- man, was charged with deserting his wife, Fanny Grace, on the 18th inst. Mr. Browne appeared for the com- plainant, and Mr. P. Davies for the defendant. He had on the previous Friday been bound over to keep the peace for assaulting her. A VIOLENT DRUNICARD.—Patrick Lavell, a navvy, was charged with being drunk and refusing to quit the Masonic Hotel, and also with wilfully damaging a win- dow worth -£1 18s. On Saturday night the prisoner went into tile hotel in a state of intoxication and when he was refused a drink, he became very violent and was ejected. He then smashed a window. He was tined in the total sum of 20s. and costs or in default 35 days' imprisonment.

div.head: EXECUTION AT DURHAM.
div.p: EXECUTION AT DURHAM.

John William Johnson, *9, farm labourer, was hanged in Durham Gaol, on Tuesday morning, for the murder of Margaret Addison, at Hetton-le-Hole, Durham. He had been living with the woman for some years, and as she contemplated matrimony with another man, Johnson overtook her in the public highway and shot her dead with a revolver. At his trial, prisoner declined counsel's aid, and pleaded guilty. He made no concealment of the fact that the deed was contemplated, and deliber- ately carried out. The condemned man rose early,when the chaplain visited him. He walked firmly to the scaffold, and as he took his place under the drop, ex- claimed, "Oh Lord! have mercy upon me. Into Thy hands I commit my spirit." The drop then fell, and death was practically instantaneous. Billington, of 80l ton, was the executioner.

CADBURY'S COCOA. is absoluttv pure.—The Public Ana- lysts have submitted CADBURY'S COCOA to close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sustain- ing and nourishing beverage. —Advt.

Three cows belonging to a small farmer at Blaton, in Belgium. were blown to pieces by means of dymanite cartridges. A workman living in the neighbourhood, who is believed to be the author of the outrage, was arrested after a desperate resistance.

At Sturry, near Canterbury, the body of an elderly lady named Sarah Flood, who was of eccentric habits' has been found in a semi-nude and extremely neglected condition. Jewellery, plate, cheques, bank notes, and other articles, value nearly £1,200, were discovered in the house.

div.head: ANOTHER CHILD MURDERED.
div.p: ANOTHER CHILD MURDERED.

Intelligence has reached Tullatnore from Clara seven miles off, that a girl named Meehan, aged six, dlughter of a Clara mechanic, was missed on Saturday night,and her dead and apparently outraged body was subse- quently found near the railway station. A man named Campbell, who had lodged with the child's father, but had decamped, has been arrested on 6uspicion. It is alleged that marks resembling blood stains were found upon his clothes.

Two annual returns just 'issued from the Board of Trade, by order of the House of Commons, one relating to authorised gas undertakings carried on by companies, and the other dealing with gas works in the hands of local authorities, give a comprehensive view of prices paid for gaslight throughout the country, The two re- turns contain the particulars of 594 undertakings, 416 being those of companies, and 178 of local authorities. The total capital actually employed in these gas enter- prises is £61,344,357, and the gross profit made last year was £2,754,473 by the companies, and £1,396,569 by the local authorities. The general figures will im- press the reader with the large proportions of the gas making business, but owing to the varying cost of coals and labour a general return of the prices charged would not be of much practical value. The figures for a county, h3wever, where the conditions are to a great extent similar, afford a guide as to the reasonableness of the price in different localities. Annexed is a tabulated view of the price charged to private consumers by all the authorised gas undertak- ings in this county giving the charges of the companies first and then of the local authorities. In addition to the price to private consumers, we give three other items which immediately influence the prices Namely, the discount allowed. the \illuminating power, and the number of consumers. FOOTBALL.

Two of the five League matches of Saturday last may have an important bearing on the championship. One of the four clubs supposed to be in tlie running had bo be satisfied with a draw, while another was beaten. Aston Villa lost their game at Wolverhampton, and can hardly now hope to make their way to the top. The Bolton Wanderers were victorious at West Bromwich, but could not repeat their success. This was partly due to ineffective forward play and partly to the magnificent defence of the Albion. Reader's gosakeeping was quitoe out of the common, and his play was greatly admired. The Wanderers have still a strong lead, but they have got through more matches than Sunderland and North End, one of which teams it is believed, will be hailed champions at the close of elle season.

Two of the Lancashire clubs were on visits in the midlands. Burnley just beat Derby County by a goal, this being their first success away from home. Stohe despatched Accrington with comparative ease, the visi- tors flout rank shaping very poorly indeed. Blackburn Rovers appeared at Trent Bridge, and may be said lso have done well in making a draw with Notts County. The Rovers are still without M'Keown, one of their full backs, and he is not likely to turn out again before the cup tie v. Derby County. Quite a number of the League Clubs changed places on Saturday, Accrington having now descended to the bottom of the table.
The second rate eleven that did battle for England were vastly superior tg the Canadians, whose long list of matches played includes a large number of defeats.

The important match which came off at Newcastle on Saturday was satisfactory in a double sense. First, because the day was in every way favourable to a trial of strength between the rival divisions ; and, secondly, because the North demonstrated their superiority for the second successive year most unmistakably. The result might well have been different, seeing that the South established a lead by a goal in the early portion of the game • but their opponents were in no way discon- certed, and as time went on tbeir prospects improved, the issue being a decisive victory for the Northerners. It is not often that there is se much scoring in a match of first importance, and the successful place-kicking was another striking feature. Indeed in the whole series of engagements there were never so.tnany goals obtained , before in any one fixture.

The North,as usual,carried the day:inthe scrimmages, the Lancashire and Yorkshire contingents doing their work splendidly. For those who have followed his career closely it is a pleasure to know that Pyke, the St. Helens Recreation man, acquitted himself so well that he was afterwards selected to represent England against Wales. Bullough, too, did well, scoring one of the tries,and he is included in the English team. Tutu Kent, who was not in the North team, has also been chosen, Toothill. of Bradfoid, being likewi.e given a place, although he had been passed over for the lievicaStle match.

Houghton was a distinct success as full back for the wirmers,and yet he has been shelved in favour of Thom- son, of Blackheath. There was no three-quarter equal to Lockwood, who ran in twice and placed two capital goals. His all round display was admirable. Taylor made a great impression, and it is not surprising to find that he and Briggs, who was also successful, are the half backs to play against Wales. Alderson varied con- siderably,but he was safe as a whole. The match was a very enjoyable one,tbroughout.

The Rugby! Union Committee, after the decision of North v. South match, selected the following fifteen to represent England v. Wales, at Blackheath. on January 2nd :—England.—W. B. Thomson (Blackheath), back; R. E. Lockwood (Yorkshire), F. R. Alderson (Durham!), and C. G. Hubbard (Kent), three-quarters; W. Taybr (Northumberland) and A.Brigas kYorkshire),lialf-backs ; W. Yiend (Gloucestershire), L. R. Percival (Oxford), F. Evershed (Midland Counties). W. Nicholl (Yorkshire), W. B. Bromet (Yorkshire), J. Toothill (Yorkshire), X. Bullougha.:Pyke,>nd T. Kent (Lancashire), forwards.

A return match was played by the Lancashire and Camhridge University teams on Monday at Whalley Range. A dense fog prevailed in Manchester and the neighbourhood before noon, but it then lifted, and all doubt as to the match taking place was setaside, and the covering of hay was removed from the field. Much vahs- abletime was however, lost, and the kick off was delayed half-an-hour, the result being that the greater portion of the second half was played in a thick fog which had re- appeared when the sun set, and made it almost impossible to follow the game or distinguish the players. The ground was in good condition, and the earlier stages of the match, were, especially from a Lancashire point of view, pleasant and enjoyable. The first match at Cern- bridge was won by Lancashire with 18 points to 10, but the Light Blues have since then beaten the sister Univer- sity of Oxford, and it was expected that they would at least show a bold front to the County Palatine. They, however, entirely failed to do so, and were outplayed throughout the game at all points and defeated by this crushing majority of 25 points to two. In the Lanca- shire team were J. T. Bate, of Warrington, and W. Cross, St. Helens,at half-back, and J. Pyke, of St. Helens Recs. in the forwards, and all these local players did well for their side.

div.head: DEATH OF COLONEL HARCOURT.
div.p: DEATH OF COLONEL HARCOURT.

The death is announced of Colonel Edward W. Harcourt, late member of Parliament for the County of Oxford, and elder brother of Sir William Vernon Harcourt. The deceased, who died on Saturday, at his seat Nuneham.Park, Abingdon,was born in 1825, and was first returned for Oxfordshire in 1878. His only son and heir, Mr. Aubrey Harcourt, is absent with Lord Sheffield in Australia. Sir William Har- court was in attendance on his elder brother in his last illness.

The Harcourts are paternally Vernons. The second son of the first Lord Vernon became Arch- bishop of York, and inheriting through his mother the estates of the Harcourts in Oxfordshire as- sumed their name in addition to hii own. The archbishop's grandson, Colonel Harcourt, now de- ceased, was a quiet, amiable, retiring gentleman, a strong Tory, and devoted to his home, his books, and his farm. His delicious place, Nuneham, near Abingdon, is endeared to every Oxford man by the memories of water parties and picnics. Is is an open secret that for some years the tw.o brothers were not on the best of terms, but their differences were happily settled some time siiice,and Sir WM. Harcourt was at Nuneham at the time of his brother's death. 31r. Harcourt leaves only two children, a son who succeeds to the estates, and who is unmarried, the lady to whom he was engaged one of the daughters of the Dean of Christ Church, dying suddenly shortly before the date fixed for the wedding. Thus between Sir William and the Nune- ham estates there is at present but one life. 'Mr. Harcourt's daughter is the Countess of Winch elsea. Despite the jeers at Sir W. Harcour.t as the descen- dent of the Plantaganets, the family to which he belongs is one .of the oldest and tne,t illustrous in the the kingdom, for the Harcourts undoubtedly came over with the conqueror, and can reckon among their members many illustrious men, relics of whom may be seen at IN uneham.

DEATH OF THE DUKE OF DEVONSHIRE.

The Duke of Devonshire died on Monday night, at eight o'clock. His grace passed away peacefully without pain, in the presence of all the members of his family, including Lord Harlington and Lady- Louisa Illzerton, his only living son and only daugh- ter, for whom great sympathy and feeling is felt by all the people of Furness and North Lancashire, to whom they are much endeared. The Duke had been in feeble health for a considerable time, and was taken suddenly worse on the 4th inst., when the Marquis of Hartington gave up a political en- gagement at Bacup,and at once proceeded to biker Hall, where he remained until the duke breathed his last. Dr. Beardsley was unremitting to his atten- tion upon the aged patient from the moment his condition became criiical. His Grace is succeeded by the Marquis of Haitington, who now enters the Upper House, thereby causing a vacancy in the Parliamentary representation of the Rossendale Division of North-East Lancashire The late Duke was the seventh of his line, and was born in 1808. He was educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he graduated second wrangler and Smith's prizeman at the age of twenty-one. He after- wards became Chancellor w: the Universities of London and Cambridge. The Cavendish family, who were en- nobred by James 1., have played a great part in the biat ,ry of their country, the first peer being the son of William Cavendish, the geutleman usher to Cardinal Wolsey, while his dessendants from time to time occu- pied some of the first positions in the State. The num- ber of residences belonging to the Devonshires are more numerous than thos2 of any other family, including royalty. Devonshire House, Piccadilly, Hardwick Half, andrhatsworth, in Derbyshire, Bolton Abbey and Skip- ton, in Yorkshire, Holker Hall, in Westmoreland, and Lismore Castle, near Waterford, are ameng the few of the best known, but perhaps the most favoured of his dwellings was that at Eastbourne. The Duke's great bobby of cattle-raising had made him very popular with the agricultural element, and there was no more regular visitor t,.-) the annual Cattle Show, Islington, than his Grace, who gained the sobriquet of " The Prince of gentlemen farmers." Lord Hartingt on's translation to the House of Lords as Duke of Devonshire leaves Mr. Chamberlain in supreme command of the Liberal Unionists in the Commons. Already Lord Hartington had remitted the active work of leadership to his colleague, only intervenino, with his weighty counsel on occasions of high importance. Next there is a vacancy in the representation of the Enssen- dale Division. In 1835 Lora Eartington defeated a Con- servative by 1,878. In 1886 he defeated a Gladstonian by 1,453. The 1886 poll was 940 below that of 1885..

(From the "Star.") Lord Hartington and his father have been alike in one thing. Both owe their position to the death of a brother. The Earl of Burlington's eldest son was thrown from his horse and killed when the Duke of Devonshire was a boy of four, and the Duke's eldest on also died young, mak- ing all the difference to both between the portion- of a younger son and the possession of three hundred square miles of territory and £200,000 a year. Derbyshire is still the backbone of the wealth of the Cavendishes. They own nearly ninety thousand acres in the county, with a rent-roll of more than £BO,OOO a year; but of late the Lancashire and Sussex estates have grown enor- mously in value. Barrow and Eastbourne, are almost entirely on the Duke's property, and few English towns can be compared with either of them in the rapidity of their rise. The Duke of Devonshire also owns estates in sight other English caunties, and in three Irish counties as well. The Duke has been unlike most ground landlords in one respect. He has from the first given his town leaseholders the option of buying the freeholds at thirty years' purchase. This is one reason of the growth 'of Eastbourne. Two years ago, out of two thousand three hundred houses built on the Duke's land, one thousand four hundred and six had been redeemed, and five hun- dred and thirty-six were in process of redemption. The Duke has spent freely on improvements in Eastbourne. He built a sea wall two miles long. Which cost £300,000, and when the local board were carrying out a drainage scheme, he spent .P.Ao,clog more in carrying the outfall three miles away. The walks and promenades from the Wish Tower slopes to the foot of Beachy Head, involved him in an outlay of £50,000. Two years ago he offered control of these lovely walks to the Eastbourne Corpora- tion, and last year he made a further offer to extend the Parade eastward, to form pleasure grounds, and to con- struct a marine drive to Pevensey. His Barrow improve- ments have been of a different sort, but have been effective in improving the industrial capacities of the town. There is no pretence that this has been done for philanthrophic reasons, or that it is more than the com- mercal policy of a long-headed man who can afford to watt for certain returns. Holker Hall has for many years been the Duke's favourite residence. Chatsworth was too much of a show place to suit his simple tastes. Hardwick Hall is much more homely, although the furnishings and hang- ings are so old-world, but this has long been set apart for Lord Hartington. Lismore Castle, the lovely Irish home of the family on the Blackwater, in Waterford County, was occasionally visited before Lord Frederick Cavendish's death, but since then the late Lord Edward has been its only occupant. But at Holker the Duke was at once the patriach and companion of his children and grandchildren. It is an unpretending,homely house, with rocky heights in the park commanding ex- tensive views over the sands of the river Leven. The Duke has always spent Christmas at Holker, and for nearly eighteen months it has been his constant home. Devonshire House, in Piccadilly, is not the only Lon- don house of the Cavendishes. They also own Chiswick House, which it was lately in the Duke's mind to sell. Fox and, Canning both died at Chiswick House, and its grounds ware the scene of many famous al fresco enter- tainments early in the century. A gloom has settled on Devonshire House. The gates are seldom open, and although the house is the scene of occasional bazaars,its forbidding aspect prevents many people inspecting the glories of its white marble staircase and dark ballroom. Like the Duke of Cleveland,the Duke's cousin and prede- cesaor could dispose of his estates as he liked. The en- tail had been cut off, and his father died before the re- settlement, but everything was left to the heir. A Barrow correspondent says the funeral will take place on Saturday afternoon, at half-past two o'clock, at Edensor. The Duke of Devonshire and the other members of the family arrived at Chatsworth on Tuesday. It was the wish of the late duke that he should be buried in Edensor Churchyard, in a grave next to that of the late Lord Frederick Cavendish. It will be a plain earth grave. Edensor Church is about a mile and a quarter from Chatsworth. On Tuesday, the bereaved family at Holker Hall receivoi scores of telegrams from all parts of the country in terms of condolence at the death of the late Duke of Devonshire. These include sympathetic Messages from the Queen, the Prince of Wales, the Duke of Connaught, the Duk'e of Fife, and conspicuous mem- bers of the great political parties.

A 'REPLY TO MR. FOULKES.

Sir,—ln replying to the letter of your correspondent, Robert Foulkes, I wish to point out to him that he seems to belabouring under a mistake in asserting that there was no such official as a priest in the Christian ministry at the time of the apostles. Now if Mr. Foulkes reads Ins Bible as much as he would have us believe he does be will find theta he turns to Acts-14 chap., v. 22 mention is made therein concerning them. I also wish to inform Mr. Foulkes that there is also such a person as a deacon, as the name occurs in the same book chap. 6 V. 5. I cannot properly understand what Mr. Foulkes means when he says there was no such person is a bishop mentioned at that time, when he should know, or ought to have known, that at that time St. James was Bishop of Jerusalem and martyred there, A.D. 62. He also asserts that no mention is made of confirmation. But if be 'reads well the Acts of the Apostles he will find it mentioned there very often. Mr. Foulkes seems to be greatly inconsed about the decorations of God's altar at Christmas time. Now if a member of the royal family were to visit the place Mr. Foulkes belongs to, no doubt Mr. Foulkes would be one of the first to show his loyalty to his Queen and country by decorating or helping to decorate his house, &c. If Mr. Foulkes would show so much respectto an earthly Queen or ping how much more exilic' he show his respect to tne coming of the King of Heaven P Would Mr. Foulkes begrudge us the laying out of a few pence in order to show our respect to the coming of one far dearer to us Christians than any earthly king or queen-? I for one should say not. It would be more charitable and more Christian like on the part of Mr. Foulkes if he wsuld save his condemna- tory remarks about any paper publishing what it thinks to be right for the good of its readers, and to keep out .of print altogether, if he cannot be sure of what he says or can only write to contradict others.—l remain, &c., J. T. C. C.
MR. PEERS AND THE QUESTION OF EVOLUTION.

have read with considerable interest the discus- Isions which have recently taken place in your columns, Anil especially those in which Mr. J. Peers has figured-so copzpicuously. Mr. Peers is a doughty foeman ; ane indeed whose pen if feathered with logic is nevertheless dipped in gall. But lam glad to recognise him as one of those who, in an age of Mammon worship, have an eye for the Eternal verities. All of us, I fancy, are, in some way mother, working out the purposes of• God to larger and di4ner issues, and Mr. Peers no doubt among the number.

At present—and I must confess it—l am deriving no ,small amount of amusement from the spectacle of Mr. Teers marcting through the laud, so to speak, seeking whom he may devour and running a tilt at every wind will he comes across. Now if he wants some work, with your permission, Mr. Editor, I will fnd him some. This is a town where one soon gets rusty,and it is rather a privilege thanotherwise, to meet in discussion a gentle- man of ability and learning like Mr.. Peers. I take •itisom his letters that he is an out-and-out evolutionist. In evolutionist of this type holds firstly that life is a pro- perty—a natural evolution of organised matter ; an& secondly, that the human mind is an evolution of the nervous organisation. I will discuss the first of these
TAILORING.
TAILORING.
TAILORING.
TAILORING.
TAILORING.,

Ipropositions with him, each of us to have say four 1 letters of half a column in length, Mr. Peers taking the affirmative. It would be necessary to have the proposi- tion clearly stated,and to have an understanding that no new matter should be introduced in the last letter of each writer. I hope Mr. Peers will be able to see his way t• taking up this subject. A word or two on the importance of the subject-matter may not be out of place. Abiogenesis, or the evolution of life from the non-living.is the keystone of Agnostic and Atheistic Evolution. If life be a property of matter then what we term the " soul" of man may reasonably be considered an evolution of the complicated nervous orga- nisation of man, and immortality become a dream. If the whole of the living nature and the whole domain of mind are to be referred to purely material causes then there is no longer room or reason for God, matter being a sufficient explanation of all things. Consequently the question" Can matter, under any 'conditions, evolve life." is one of the greatest moment, demanding from all who approach it the utmost candour and the clearest thinking.—l remain yours truly, Wilderspool.
W. H. BUTLER,

THE PREVENTION OF CRUELTY TO CHILDREN. Sir,—A meeting was held in the Town Hall, on Wed- nesday, the 9th inst, called together by circular and announcement from the pulpits, to discuss the advis- ability of forming a branch of the above-named good Society, for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children., and in order to add another detective to the forces of law and order that exist to grapple with the evils of drink, selfishness, and insurance money, which appear to defy the efforts of Christian men and women, of schools, churches, and charity organisations, so numerous in our town. It is most humilating to witness the necessity of such a meeting of clergy and leading townsmen,unanim- ous in the conviction that it requires this Society to come to the rescue ofilittle children of all classes alike, whether rich or poor. The objects and motives of these cruelties appear to be chiefly due to the saving or the making of money, and not so much to passion or wanton neglect. The rev. gentleman (Mr. Waugh), in his answers tl my questions as to the number of cases of starvation and murders committed in order to obtain insurance money, was very vague, and was not reliable in his in- formation, inasmuch as the 1,276 or 12,076 cases, he is reported to have stated, cannot all be laid at the doors of insurance companies and societies, unless he can prove the children to have been murdered entirely to get the insurance money. I think the statement he has made is a very serious one, for insurance men to reflect upon. He replied, that in twelve months, he may come again to surprise us with a report of his detective, who will ' be commissioned to unravel the "insurance horrors" of our town. I will promise him a most difficult task in find- ing out conspiracies, connivances, and secrecies always found among the insuring public. I was glad to find the rev, gentleman is no respecter of persons, although, he, like General Booth, appeals to the rich., for ,(as he said at the meeting) " those thundering big figures." I doubt not he respects the decent artisan and his wife, and the devoted mothers of well cared-for children, and would not think £6 too much to decently inter any child. The rev, gentleman's reply was reported as 12,076 cases of starvation, triceable to insurance, while another states 1,276 cases a difference of 10,800. I really wonder which was right. lam sure oi4e reporter made a great mistake in stating that I was satisfied with the answers given ; I never did say that they were satisfac- tory. If the rev, gentleman's observations are so keen as only to see the little children suffer, and not the aged and feeble, in a like position, who are more the objects of higher speculation than puny children, who are protected by law and limited to small sums, then, I say, if a society like this; is demanded for the young, I would suggest that something be done for the old, and, if the rev, gentleman will not do it, I hope a small committee, or band of Christian men may be formed in every town each to act the part of detective, in his spare moments and to go behind the scenes, and note the abuses which exist, such information to be used at the proper time. I believe such a movement will be a healthy check on speculation on human life, and instead of being an hindrance to the honest insurance offices, superintend- ents and agents, it would help them to get honest con- tracts, and purge forgers from insurance business.— Yours, &c. JOHN MOORFIELD. 44 Parker-st., Warrington, December, 1891.

div.head: DOCTRINES OF THE CHURCH.
div.p: THE DOCTRINES OF THE CHURCH.

Sir,—ln a recent issue:Mr. Robert Foulkes " begs to differ" from the Rector of Warrington. He is quite a little Pope in his way; let us see if he be not even more fallible than he would doubtless allow Leo XIII to be. Take his first point; article xix., says "The visible Church of Christ is a congregation of faithful:men, &c. This beings°, there must be a visible rite by which men become members of it—leaving out the disputed point of infant baptism altogether. Baptism is this rite. The form of baptism in th. " 0-mmon Prayer dis- tinctly teach that baptism is the entrance into the church; see the first 'prayer after the opening exhorta- ion. See also:S. John iii. 5., S. Matt. xxviii 19, and 1. Peter 3. 21. At any rate Mr. Foulkes need not object to the Rector's statement, for according to the Gorham judgment they are both right, a very comforting thing for them to think of as members of a teaching church which " hath authority in controversies of faith '' and accordingly decides that two opposite beliefs are both right. Then take Confirmation. According to article xxv. it is either "a corrupt following of the Apostles," or is a "state of life allowed in the Scriptures." It very , plainly is not a state of life; end if it be a "corrupt fol- lowing of the Apostles" and unscriptural, why confirm people at all and why make it a compulsory preliminary to admission to Communion? See rubric at end of Con- firmation service. See also Acts viii. 15-18. Verse 18 is especially conclusive on this sacrament. I suppose Mr. Foulkes would consider the Church to have been too corrupt in the year 100 A.D., but earlier even than this, St. Clement wrote—" All must make haste to be confirmed by a bishop -; that is, to receive the sevenfold grace of the Holy Ghost "—Epistola ad Julium. We cannot hut admit that the Church of England has certainly departed from primitive doctrine in degrading confirmation from its sacramental position. Mr. Foulkes is presumably a Churchman, and as his church is Epis- copal in government, his objoction to Episcopacy seems rather pointless. See I Tim. 1, 7. As to confession, see end of first exhortation in the communion service; also "Visitation of the sick," prov- ing that confession to a priest is allowed in the Church of England under certain circumstances; it has, how- ever, been formally discountenanced by several bishops a few years ago; another case of black being white. The scriptural proofs of confession are conclusive to an unprejudiced mind; see St. John xx. 7-3, St. Matt. xviii. 18, Acts xix. 18 19, St. James v. 16, and the constant practice of the Catholic Church for 19 Centuries. The "long usage" argument is largely used by Churchmen when arguing in favour of tithes, and ought to recom- mend itself to Mr. Foulkes on the subject of confession. As to the Real Presence, he really scores a point in quoting the 'black rubric," but even this is somewhat balanced by the catechism "What is the inward part or thing signified ?'' "The body and blood fif 'Christ, which are verily and indeed taken and received by the faithful in the Lord's Supper." But of course we cannot be sur- prised at the Church of England allowing contrary be- liefs on such a momentous doctrine as the Real Presence. Aithough, presumably a Churchman, Mr. Foulkes ven- tures to place his interpretation of Scripture against that of his Church, and he may find reference to the follow- ing passages of great interest: St. John vi. 32-58, Matt. xxvi. 26-29. and St. Luke xxii. 15-20. These rival Churchmen will never find unity of doctrine unless they give up the false system of private judgment in inter- pretation of the Scriptures, and submit to the one and only Church of Christ with its visible head in the chair of Peter.—Yours faithfully, WALTER POULTON. 94, Kingsley-road, Liverpool.

THE WORLD'S F AIR AT CHICAGO.—The remarkable run of 4384 miles in 4251 minutes on the New York Cen- tral and Hudson River Railway Company has put other American railway managers on their mettle, and they are now preparing for the expected large traffic to the Chicago World's Fair in 1893. This Railway,whick,iike :our own London and North-Western and Midland, has Always been the pioneer of improvement, is making •-strong efforts to provide further accommodation thronet- • out their system, which is the natural route to Chicago and the West. This is the only line out of New YOfic which daily runs five great trains to the West, at an average speed 0150 miles an hour, with all the luxurious! appointments which can add to the comfort and con-, •venience of passengers. The improvement in the perma- nent way and the development of speed have done much to increase the traffic between this country and the great -West, whilst the danger of fast running has di- nlinisbek the gradients being easy and the route nearly level. 'Passengers can now breakfast at New York and dine at 'Niagara Falls. Chicago is reached in 24 hours, St. Louis in 32, Cincinnati:in 24,and Montreal in 12. The I Company also runs daily throughout the year, the Empire State Express," which is " vestibuled" all through, and is heated by steam and lighted by gas. The Company is represented in Europe by Messrs. Thomas Meadows, & Co., Liverpool, London, Manchester, Glas- gow, and Paris.

A Happy New Year to yo'. Last week aw took th' liberty o' wishin' yo' a Merry Kesmas, but this week aw tak a gretter liberty becose Kesmas nobbut lasts a day, an' th' New Year is new for at leeast a month. Aw'll ad- mit as id is a liberty, speykin' to strangers, an' swappin' th' compliments o'th' seeason ; but they o' do id. Even th' parson o' yo'r district, as ne'er speyks to yo' at ony other time, manages to screw his face up into wod he thinks th' perfect imitation ov a smile, an' he nods an' says "A Happy New Year to you " ; then he goes on his way varry weel suited wi' hisser at hevin' done sich a benevolent an' agreeable, an' seeasonable action. Well, wishes are nod lika cosses as coom hoome to roost, an' ther may be a bit o' sincerity i' these wishes o' mine. In fact—just in a whisper—aw may say as aw meean every syllable o' wod aw say ; yo an' me are varra like fooak ridin' in a railway carriage together. Aw do o'tle tawkin' an' aw'm nod beawn to say as it's full o' sense, or witty, or owt o' thad sorrt ; but 8G wod id is it's like th' tawk o' mony a chap i' th train,an' whether wise or foolish we may learn sum- mat fro' id. lv one or two remerks is th' result o' years o' experience they're vallyable to some chap or woman as may happen to hear 'em just at th' reight time; id may be a remerk as exaggerates 801128 failin or other, or a fau't, an' th' failin' an' fau't wod'ud ha' seemed sich—or shown up as plain—beawt a bit o' magnifyin'. Onyway, id draws one's attention to id, an' a bit o' thiukin' o'er id often ends in id bein' remedied. Well, th' year end is a grand time to co' attention to past mistakes, an' it's th' time when mooast fooak mek up their minds to profit by 'ern through th' comin' year. Listen wod thad blood- thirsty humourist Thomas of Richards of Roberts , hes to say on th' subject.

WHBN '92 COMES IN. There's molly a one—o' ayther sex— Reawever bad they'n bin Some random resolution meks, Afoore th' new year cornea in. There's fooak 'at's drunk,'o' thro' this year Resolvin' to begin To keep away fro' stuff like beer When '92 comes in. There's chaps 'at's bet on mony a hoes, An' lost no end o' tin, Resolvin' nod to risk one loss When '92 comes in, There's fooak 'at's gossipt fro' their youth, An lied to mates an' kin, Declare they'll tell nowt else but truth When '92 comes in. An everybody 'at's done owt .I'th' way o' gradely sin. Say as they'll nevermoore be nowt When '92 comes in. Ay, well, ne'er gawm 'em wod they say, For them as meks mooast din— Their grand resolves 'll"breyk tost day As '92 comes in. Thad last verse is rather severe, wod ?

Sit yo' deawn bi th' fire, leet yo'r pipe, an' between whiffs try iv yo' con ged a glent o' owt silly as yo've done i'th year just endin'; owt as yo' wodn'd keer to do o'er ageean th' year as is comiff. Happen yo'v dropt a bit o' brass in a foolish spec, an' iv id isn'd o' as yo' hev, or iv yo' hey health an' strength, be thankful. There hes bin cases latly wheere varra owd fooak hes lost every Denny they hed th' world, an' nowt but th' werkheawse stares 'era th' face; yo' hey a hooam—" be it ever so humble " an' a wife an' family to comfort yo'. Th' pill may be a bitter un to swallow, but id'll porge yo' ov a lot o' nonsense. Yigh, happen o' yo'r chronic greed as wed; aw'm capt at fooak bein' so silly as to put their herd-earned savin's th' hands o' ony plau- sible waistrel as offers five per cent. Aw thowt th' confidence trick hed bin played eawt long sin', but it's still runnin' merrily an' attractin' big audiences; well, experience meks foo's wise.
But 'cod abeawt thad last verse? Well, aw nobbut want to say as a hen does id cacklin' at after it's laid id egg, an' nod afoore.

Fro' wod aw con mek eawt th' fost month o' th' year is kessened after an owd chap o' th' name o' Janus; he were two-faced, an' there's a lot OY his descendants alive this varra minute. One o' these faces looks back'ards i' a pleessed look, an' t' other looks forrud wi' a puzzled sort o' look, as iv id dudn'd know wod were beawn to happen next. This Janus is said to represent Noah, one o' th' faces lookin' back to th' flood, an' t' other lo)kin' to— wel!, aw dorn'd know wod. A tooathri centuries kesseird Jennewarry " the wolf- month," an' aw think t lit's a varra sensible name, becose th' middle o' th' winter is abeawt th' time as th' wolf comes to th' door. Th' question is heaw to freeten id away! Wod weapon to use to id? To mooast fooak aw con safely recommend: A temperance club! Temkin' abeawt lookin' back'ard reminds, me o' this passage aw were readin' i'th book o' thad name last neet. "Men lov'd women in those days, as now. God knows how they dared be fathers, but they had babies as sweet, no doubt, to them as ours to us, whom they must feed, clothe,educate. The gentlest creatures are fierce when they have young to pro- vide for, and in that Wolfish Society the struggle for bread borrowed a peculiar desperation from the tenderest sentiments. For the sake of those depend- ent upon him, a man might not choose, but must plunge into the tool fight—cheat, overreach, sup- plant, defraud, buy below worth and sell above, break down the business by which his neighbour fed his young ones, tempt men to buy what they •ought not and to sell what they should not, grind his labourers, sweat his debtors, cozen his credit- ors. Though a man sought it carefully with tears,it was hard to find a way in which he could earn a liv- ing and provide for his family except by pressing in 'before some weaker rival and taking the food from his mouth. Even the ministers of religion were not • exempt from this cruel necessity!' That's suppoased to be "seem' eawrsels as others see us " Anno Domino 2,000. Heaw sid strike yo'? Aw wonder iv thad bit hes out to do wi' General Booth as mentions ministers o' religion tekkin' th food fro other meawths ! Id looks as iv id rapt him on th' knackles for undersellin' wi' his Salvation firewood, or Hallelujah firewood, as they happen co' id. Chaps, do sit deawn next Thorsda' Peet abeawt eleven o'clock an' think like beggary till th' bells tune up; then pike off to bed, an' sleep o'er id. It's nobbut bi tekkin stock keerfully as yo' con find eawt heaw mich ye' are to th' bad, an' then yo',mon try an' find eawt why yo're thad mich. Profit bi th' lesson. ANV know one's life coiled be assesseel bi a tooathri figures put under .£ an' S. an' D.; wife an childer an' friends, an' th' mutual love between yo an' them are summed up different nor wi' peaw ads, shillin's an' pence. But to see 'em sufferin' through past errors, or neglect, or owt as could ha' bin helpt bi a bit o' t ! Well,s Happy New Year to us o'.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
THE NEW BILL AND HOW IT WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON DOCKS.

The new Bill which is being promoted in Parliament by the Manchester Ship Canal Company was deposited on Monday as required by the standing orders of the House of Commons. Some of the provisions of the Bill, which refer to the construction of the proposed docks, affect the interests of Warrington to an important degree. In the preamble to the Bill the docks are re- ferred to in the following terms:—" And whereas by sub-section 6 of section 88 of the Act of 1885 it was pro- vided that the Company should complete the Warrington Dock (being dock No. 4, work No. 13, by that Act authorised) within the period of three years after the contpletion of the Canal between- Eastham and Latch- ford : And whereas the period limited by the Act of 1885 for the completion of the works by that Act authorised was seven years from the passing of the Act which period was by the Manchester Ship Canal Act 1891 ex- tended until the 31st day of December 1893, and it is expedient that the said period limited for the completion of the said dock should be extended until the 31st day of December 1895."

According to the above preamble the desire of the Company is to obtain an extension of the time for the completion of the Warrington docks from December 1893 to December 1895, but the clause in the Act itself bearing upon the Matter is not quite so specific, and in addition to that it contains a proviso which is of the greatest importance to this locality. Section 21 of the Bill read as follows :—" That notwithstanding anything contained in the section 39 (period for completion of works) and section 88 (for the protection of Corporation and traders &c. of Warrington) of the Act of 1885 and section 12 (extension of time for completion of works) of the Act of 1891, the time for the completion of the Warrington Dock is hereby extended to the period of three years from the completion and opening for traffic of the portion of the canal between Ea.stham and Latch- ford and front and after the expiration of that period the power to constrzct that dvck shall cease." It would seem from the words given in italics that the company are not merely seeking for an extension of the time within which they are ta construct the docks, but they are also providing for themselves a loophole by means of which they may abandon the docks altogether if they should think it desirable to do so hereafter. If the section quoted is sanctioned by Parliament, it seems clear that all the company would need to do, in order to shuffle out of their engagement to make docks at War- rington, would be to delay,on one pretext or another, or on no pretext at all,the carrying out of the work till the end of the three years extension of time, and then they would be even without the power to complete the docks.

The Bill affects another part of the Canal Company's scheme in the neighbourhood of Warrington. It will be remembered that the original proposal of the company included the diversion of the Mersey just below the Arpley irogpbriclge, and this proposal has been so far car- ried out that the new bed of the river has been made though the stream does not as yet low through it. The diversion will be effected by the making of a dam across the river channel at the end of River-st.,off Wilderspool- road, and it was intended to make another dam at the other end of the river diversion opposite Lower Walton. Power is now sought, however, to abandon this latter dam, and to make one in its place farther up the river, near Tom Paise's bridge. In consequence of this alteration the intended new road across Arpley Meadows will have to be taken over the river, near Lower Walton, by an iron bridge of the same height as that at Walton Arches. By this new arrangement a shorter length of the river bed will be enclosed between the two dams, but between this enclosed length of river and the Ship Canal there will be a channel of com- munication whereby vessels may pass from one to the other. The lower dam, that near Tom Paine's bridge, will be furnished with locks to enable vessels to pass from the enclosed to the unenclosed parts of the river, or vice versa, so that there will still be a means of communication for vessels between the river and the Ship Canal. Judging from these proposals it might be surmised that the intention of the Ship Canal Company is not to deprive Warrington altogether of its docks, but to provide no more dock accommoda- tion—at least for an indefinite time to come—than is to be found in the enclosed portion of the river bed. It is to be borne in mind, of course, that so long as the neces- sary means of communication between the canal and the river are made in the first instance there will always afterwards he the possibility of enlarging the dockage to the extent that the growth of traffic might render desirable.

div.head: CHRISTMAS HOLIDAYS.
div.p: THE CHRISTMAS HOLIDAYS.
The employes of the Ship Canal Company left work on Thursday at a quarter-past twelve for the Christmas holidays, and return on Tuesday morning. '
THELWALL MISSION HALL.

A special service was given in the Ship Canal Mission Hall on Sunday evening. A band of 18 was in attend- ance. Mr. H. Horner conducting. After the first lesson had been read, the" Magnificat " was sung, the "Nunc Dimittis " following the second lesson. A solo, "Eternal rest," was tastefully rendered by Miss Silverton. The Preacher was the Hon. and Rev. R. Grimston. MORE SEIEBEENING BY NAVVIES. SEIZURE OF LIQUOR AT EASTHAM.

On Monday afternoon, Chief Superintendent Hindley of the Cheshire Police, stationed at Birkenhead, along with Sergeants Pearson and M'Cain, and a number of constables, made a raid on some of the huts occupied by, the Ship Canal navvies at Eastham, where it was sus- pected drink was sold without a license. In three of the huts a large quantity of beer and spirits was seized and removed to Birkenhead by the constables. The raid was made under the powers of search warrants, the police having had reason to believe for some time past that shebeening on an extensive scale was being carried on among the navvies at Eastham.

div.head: ALLEGED STABBING BY A WOMAN AT WIDNES,
div.p: ALLEGED STABBING BY A WOMAN AT WIDNES,

On Monday, at the Widnes Police Court,- before Mr. H. Gaskell, jun., John Kelly and his wife Jane Kelly, of 4, Legii-street, were charged in custody with causing grevious bodily harm to a man named Michael Walsh, Midwood-street, on Saturday last, by stabbing him. Superintendent Keighley said the prosecutor went home from his work about noon on Saturday, and in the afternoon he met the male prisonor in a public-house in Lugsdale. They were drinking together all afternoon, and about seven o'clock the male prisoner invited the prosecutor to his house. Walsh went there, and when they had been in the house a few minutes the female prisoner went for some drink, the prosecutor paying for it with the only money he had. Directly after the female prisoner returned the two men quarrelled. A fight ensued, and it is alleged the knife (produced' was used.—Dr. Hudson said he saw the injured man Walsh on Saturday night, and he was suffering from a wound an inch and a half long, just above the elbow of the left arm. There was also a wound on the back of the head— a cut right down to the bone. The wound on the arm was a serious one, and the man was in a dangerous condi- tion.—Polico-Sergeant Strickland said he took the two pri- soners to see Walsh on Tuesday morning, and prolocutor then identified them as the persons who had wounded him. When witness showed him the knife Walsh said "Yes, that's the one she (meaning the femaleprisoner) stabbed me with."—On the application of Superintendent Keigh- ley both prisoners were remanded in custody until Thurs- day next.

The prisoners were again brought up on Thursday, when the prosecutor gave evidence. He said when he got to the prisoners' house, the male prisoner asked him if he had any money,and he replied that he had sixpence. The prisoner asked him to send for some beer, and he gave the woman sixpence, who fetched a quart of beer. They all drank of it, and then the male prisoner shut all the doors, and without any provocation, struck him with something hard on the forehead, knocking him down. While he lay on the ground, the female prisoner held a large knife over him, and said, "What are you doing here ?" at the same time stabbing him in the arm. The male prisoner then took the knife from his wife' and said to witness, "I will murder you," and stabbed him on the head. Witness wrested the knife from him and threw it across the room,and after a fearful struggle he managed to escape out of the house. The knife used, a large carving knife, was produced. Both prisoners were committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial.
Lord Randolph Churchill left Capetawn on Thursday on the Union steamer Scot, which is due at Southamp- ton on January Bth.

At Glasgow, on Monday, John Daniel got 14 days for delivering bodies from the City Poorhouse for dissection without the certificate required by the Act. The severe frost continues generally throughout the country, and in many districts was on Thursday ac- companied by a dense fog. More deaths from exposure, a number of ice fatalities, and several drowning acci- dents in ccnsequence of fog are reported. At Bamber Bridge on Wednesday, John Atherton, farm labourer, was charged with attempting to murder Elizabeth Worthington at Samlesbury. Evidence was given showing that he fired at the young woman with a revolver, and that the bullet went through her bodice and lodged in the fastening of her corset. The prisoner, who had desired to become her suitor and shot at her in a spirit of revenge, was remanded for a week.
