div.head: WARRI-\;GTON VOLUNTEERS.
div.p: WARRI-\;GTON VOLUNTEERS.
ANNUAL PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.

The annual distribution of the prizes for company shooting and the tradesmen's Christmas prizes, in connection with the Ist Battalion Prince of Wales's Volunteers, South Lancashire Regiment, took place in the Drill Hall, Warrington, on Wednesday even- ing. The hall was decorated with flags for the occasion. Major Pickmere presided, and on the platform with him were Captain and Adjutant Adam. Captain and 'Quartermaster Hutchinson, Captains Ridgway, Buckton and Gooch, Lieuten- ants Edelsten, Chorley, and Fairclough, Major Fennely, and Sergeant-Instructors Birch and Sul- livan.

Major PICKIIEnE addressing those present as brother volunteers, said he had a right to call them such,being an honorary member of the corps and an old and active member before that, now many years ago. He had been requested to preside, owing to the serious illness of Lieutenant-Colonel Bolton which prevented him from being present. He had had a letter from him requesting him to preside. He had heard a rgood account of the corps from officers—that tile men were doing well ; and he knew from appearances that they had a good staff of officers. He was very glad to see this, but he was sorry to see that the whole corps did not join in such an occasion as the present, though he had no doubt all who had to receive prizes were present. He was glad that the tradesmen of Warrington still liked to support the corps by presents of the kind which he saw before him for Christmas. They all ' knew this that the volunteers of England were a kind of insurance against foreign invasion, and ' if we had that goodness knew what would become of us with our small army. Of course we were protected by our fleets, still if some few European nations were to join together and descend on our coasts he thought the volunteers would be enough to keep them out of the country, and it was on this account that the public thought the volunteers were worthy of their sup- port, and they not only subscribed and paid rates and taxes in an indirect way for the support of the movement, but also he was glad to say, sent little prizes for those who had shown any distinguished merit. Captain and Adjutant ADAM then addressed those present. He said he was happy to say that speaking; generally the Corps had made progress during that volun- teer year, and particularly from a musketry point of view. The figure of merit, as would have been observed, from the published orders, had gone up some six points, which he thought highly creditable, taking into consider- ation the fact that the range accommodation was very poor and inadequate. Another thing they might con- gratulate themselves upon was that of 15 non-commis- sioned officers who were competitors on the visit of the district inspector of musketry, 11 got certificates of thorough proficiency and four of proficiency. He wished Colonel Greena,ll had been there that night, to address them. He was sure he regretted extremely that his engagements in London detained him. They had had a very fair camp meeting indeed that year at Black- pool. There was only one thing to mar it, and that with the death of poor Col.-Sergt. Bate. He was a most excellent officer and a man who had a great deal of interest in his work, and was fired with a very great zeal for the corps. They had lost another officer by death, Sergeant Bebbington,and lost in him a good man. As regarded the volley firing competition B Company was the winner, and that was a very creditable thing. Lord Winmarleigh gave the first prize, and after the competi- tion he wrote to his lordship to tell him the result, and received a very kind letter from him. The Adjutant then read the letter, which stated that his lordship quite coincided with him in his praise of Col.-Sergt. Spencer for the pains he had taken with his men in connection with the competition. The result of it was that the creditable score was made of 99 out of a possible 120. Referring to the camp for the coming year, the Adjutant said it was not certain whether it would be a regimental or a brigade camp, but Major-General Hall, of the north- western district had desired him to let it be known that he would be very glad if they would attend the brigade camp at Conway during Whit week. The corps was a smart one, and (the Adjutant) quite believed it would compare very favourably with many other corps that joined the brigade camp. The Adjutant concluded by wishing the corps a merry Christmas and a happy New Year. _ .

Captain RIDGWAY next spoke. He expressed his satis- faction at the winning of the volley competition prize by the B Company,and thanked Colour-Sergeant Spencer for the able manner in which he had trained his men ; it showed that after the loss of Colour-Sergeant Bate he had got another good man. The Captain read a letter he had received from Colonel Bolton, in which he wished the volunteers a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year. The Captain then referred to the difficulties the corps had laboured under during the year with regard to equipment. The previous year the Government had not advanced a sum of money to enable them to have a pro- per equipment. Since then,Mr. Stanhope, though about the best-abused than in the Ministry, had induced the Government to give the volunteer corps of the country a sum to provide equipment. The amount which the Government had harmed to them that year for equip- ment was £338, although that was not sufficient, as they had had to spend through having to provide a store room. very nearly £l5O more than they had received, that was £.l-62 for the store room and ilbUts tor equip- ment, a total of £970. The Captain complained of the inadequacy of the present range, remarking that the best thing would be to have the volunteers disbanded, unless the Government would find money for better range accommodation, which was so necessary to their efficiency. Mr. Stanhope had stated that the Govern- ment had arranged to advance money to provide ranges for the Volunteers. It had been found necessary to have £14,000 for the purpose of providing a new range for the six battalions of the regiment at Risley, and it was expected that before long that sum would be handad over : and if that were obtained, he was sure it would be admitted that a range could be established second to none in tho country. The Cheshire Lines Committee had promised to lay down a siding so that men from Warrington, Manchester, and Wigan could be put down within about a couple of hundred yards of the shooting point. The prizes were then distributed by Major Pickmere. The Major in presenting to Col.-Sergt. Spencer the silver cup presented by Mr. Woods for the highest score in the first and second competitions, taken together, at the prize meeting, complimented the recipient, and remarked that he hoped he would always have plenty of money in his pocket to fill it with good stuff to drink. (Applause.) Captain Gooca proposed a vote of thanks to Major Picktnere for his presidency over the meeting and pre- sentation of the plizes. The vote having been heartily accotded, Major PICIDIERE responded, observing that he should always have the warmest sympathy for the old Warring- ton Volunteer Corps. A vote of thanks was passed to the tradesmen for the good things they had supplied. The following is a list of the donors of the prizes for the shoating during the year :—The Right Hon. COUNTY OF CHESTER, TO WIT. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER will be holden at the CASTLE OF CHESTER, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the 4th day of January next, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the, Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelied. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hun- dreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all pri- soners committed from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester;•at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 4th day of January next, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. The Court will be Adjourned to the Court House, Nether Knutsford, on WEDNESDAY, the 6th day of Janu- ary next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. The hear- ing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Bucklow, Macclesfield, and Northwich, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners com- mitted from the last-mentioned Hundreds will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the opening of the Court on WEDNESDAY, the 6th day of January next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester. Chester, 15th December, 1891.

LATEST NEWS.

The Dowager Lady Garvag,h died on Wednesday night at Garvagh House, county Londonderry. TEIE BIARRITZ BRITISH CLUB. Mr. Gladstone and Mr. John Morley have been unani- mously elected lion, members of the British Club at Biarritz. THE NEW BISHOP OF SODOR AND MAN. The Queen has been pleased to approve the appoint- ment of the Rev. Archdeacon Stratoia, vicar of Wake- field, to the see of Sodor and Man. DELAYS ON THE RAILWAY. At Springs Branch near Wigan, on Thursday morning, several railway waggons left the line, and the traffic was further impeded by a dense fog. The London ex- press was delayed five hours. LOSS OF AN ATLANTIC LINER. Intelligence received at Lloyd's from Sicily says the steamer Spree reports that the Guion liner Abyssinia, which left New York for Liverpool on the 13th, has been destroyed by fire in latitude 49, longitude 29. 22 west ; all hands saved. The Abyssinia wasa crew steamer of 3,651 tons gross. THE CHARGES AGAINST AN M.P. Mr. Hastings, M.P., who is in custody on a charge of fraudulently converting to his own use trust moneys, was on Thursday brought before Mr. Lushington at Bow-st., and was further remanded until Friday, January. Diu prisoner, WIR) NV 4n wviaeutay suffering from great mental depression and feebleness, was placed in the dock for a moment only, and was then conveyed to Holloway. THE ROYAL MARRIAGE. DATE FIXED. The Press Association says :—" We are authorised to state that the marriage of H.R.H. the Duke of Clarence and Avondale with H.S.H. Princess Victoria May of Teck will be celebrated in St. George's Chapel, Windsor Castle, on Saturday, 27th February." After the cere- monial the bride and bridegroom will travel to London, en route for a place yet to be selected for the honey- moon. SERIOUS RAILWAY ACCIDENT. -- THREE PERSONS KILLED-14 INJURED. A terrible railway disaster occurred near Lowestoft, on Thursday evening, in which three persons were killed and twelve were injured. Two passenger trains came into collison at Barnby Junction, a station between Lowestoft and Beccles, about seven o'clock. One train from Lowestoft stood on the line, when it was fouled by the 12 30 p.m. passenger train from London. Mach damage was done to rollimg stock. Three people were killed—the driver, the guard, and a stranger from Lon- don ; and 14 were injured. ALARMING GAS EXPLOSION. A gas explosion occurred in Fountain-court, Temple, on Thursday morning in premises abutting upon Essex- st., Strand. Gas escaped from a chandelier, in a base- ment used as a library, and a young man named Bather who was removing some of the books, was seriously injured and removed to the hospital. The explosion greatly damaged inaoy of the neighbouring chambers, and hardly a window remained whole in Essex-st. which was littered with fragments of glass and splintered win- dow frames. In the Fountain-court chambers, the damage was greater, and not confined to glass, heavy doors being torn from their hinges, and shelves and other fixtures torn from their holdings. The solidity of' the buil ling prevented damage to the basement and floor above. Fire engines hastened to the place, but their services were not needed. WAR IN MEXICO.-50 KILLED. NEw YORK, FRIDAY.—It is reported from the Mexican Border that the rebel General Garsea, with 1000 men has defeated the troops of President Diaz, killing 50 of them. RAILWAY COLLISION IN AMERICA.—SEVEN KILLED. NEW YORK, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—Seven persons were killed and ten injured, by a collision which occurred last night at Hastings, on the New York Central Railway.

THE WATERFORD ELECTION. RESULT OF THE POLL. A scene of wild enthusiasm arose in the counting-room on Thursday upon the High Sheriff announcing the result, the Parnellites cheering, shouting, and waving their hats. The crowd without took up the applause, and it was echoed all along the Mall. Mr. Redmond proposed a vote of thanks to the sheriff for conducting the poll, which Mr. Davitt seconded, and at the conclusion of his speech said he would rather have lost the election than won it by a combination of terrorism and rowdyism. This observation provoked an outburst of indignation on the part of the Parnellities. They mounted the chairs and forms, yelling, hooting, and shaking their fists menacingly at Mr. Davitt above the general din and uproar. RESULT. Redmond Davitt 1,229 Majority Mr. Sampson, the newly-appointed coroner for Liver- pool, held his first inquests on Thursday ; and at the close was congratulated by several of the jurymen on the expeditious manner in which he had gone through his duties.

SECRET MEETINGS IN POLAND. --- NUMEROUS ARRESTS. A Warsaw correspondent states that a hundred arrests were made there on Sunday night.
